title: Life beyond Earth: how scientists look for signs of life on faraway worlds

summary.text: A bottle of sugar water with yeast blows up a balloon, and a bottle without yeast does nothing. You never saw the yeast. You saw only what they did to the air. Scientists hunting for life on faraway planets work in the same way, because no telescope can see a creature on a planet trillions of kilometres away. They look for the gases that life leaves behind. In this unit your child works out which bottles hold living yeast from the gas they make, finds how warm the milk must be for curd bacteria, and then asks where in space such signs might be found, and how sure we can ever be.
summary.art: Four bottles in a row with balloons on top, the balloon on the first bottle swollen and the other three flat, and a small telescope looking at a faraway planet with a faint glowing ring of air.

intro.hook: Two bottles stand on a table. They are sealed, and you cannot see through them. The balloon on one of them is slowly swelling, and the balloon on the other is flat. You cannot open them or look inside. What can you say about what is in each bottle?
intro.text: You can say that something in the first bottle is making gas, and that something in the second is not. That is exactly the problem of a scientist who studies a planet from very far away. She cannot land, scoop up soil or look at a creature. She can only read the light that comes through a planet's air. In this unit you find out which bottles hold living yeast from the gas they make, test the warmth that curd bacteria need, and learn how scientists read the air of worlds they will never visit.
intro.art: A child looking at two sealed bottles with balloons, and behind them a drawing of a distant planet with a thin ring of air.

outcomes: I can explain what makes a planet or moon a place where life could live: liquid water, energy, the right chemicals, and the right temperature.
I can explain why the habitable zone depends on the star, and why distance alone does not decide if a world is warm.
I can explain how living things can get energy from chemicals in the dark, and why that matters for Europa and Enceladus.
I can run a fair test to show that living yeast change the gas around them, and explain what a biosignature is.
I can explain how scientists find planets and read their air with light, and why a gas alone does not prove life.
I can use a chain of guesses to estimate how many civilisations there might be, and say why the answer depends on the guesses.
I can say what counts as life, and why scientists disagree about fire, viruses and crystals.
I can say what scientists agree on, what they still argue about, and how to check a news story about life in space.

terms.meaning: The ring of distances around a star where a planet with an atmosphere could be warm enough to have liquid water on its surface.
terms.example: Earth is in the Sun's habitable zone. Venus is near the hot inner edge and Mars is near the cold outer edge.
terms.art: A star in the middle with a ring around it coloured green, with a hot inner zone in red and a cold outer zone in blue.

terms.meaning: The layer of gases that surrounds a planet or moon, held by its gravity.
terms.example: Earth's atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Venus has a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A blue planet with a thin glowing layer of air around it.

terms.meaning: The warming of a planet when gases in its air hold back some of the heat that tries to escape into space.
terms.example: Venus's thick carbon dioxide makes it the hottest planet, hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun.
terms.art: Sunlight coming down into a planet's air, and heat arrows trying to leave but bouncing back.

terms.meaning: An invisible shield around a planet that bends away fast particles from the Sun. Earth has one because of the metal moving deep inside the planet.
terms.example: Earth's magnetic field helps to keep our air from being blown away by the solar wind, the stream of fast particles from the Sun.
terms.art: Earth with curved lines of a magnetic field and arrows of solar wind bending around it.

terms.meaning: Making food from chemicals, not from sunlight. Some bacteria do this, for example from hydrogen sulfide gas. Say it like this: kee-moh-SIN-thuh-sis.
terms.example: Bacteria at deep-sea vents make food from chemicals in the hot water, and tube worms live on that food.
terms.art: A tube worm beside a hot vent on the dark sea floor, with tiny bacteria drawn inside the worm.

terms.meaning: A crack in the sea floor where water heated deep underground rushes out, carrying dissolved chemicals.
terms.example: Life thrives around hydrothermal vents in the dark deep sea, where sunlight never reaches.
terms.art: A black chimney on the sea floor pouring out dark hot water, with white crabs and red worms around it.

terms.meaning: A sign that living things have been there. It may be a gas, a chemical, a shape or a pattern that is hard to explain without life.
terms.example: A balloon swelling on a bottle of yeast and sugar is a biosignature of living yeast.
terms.art: A balloon swelling on a bottle, with a magnifying glass over the balloon.

terms.meaning: Light spread out into its colours, like a rainbow. A gas takes away its own colours from light, so a spectrum shows which gases the light passed through.
terms.example: Light from a star that passes through a planet's air has dark gaps in its spectrum for each gas in the air.
terms.art: A rainbow strip with several thin dark lines across it, and labels pointing to the gases that made them.

terms.meaning: A planet that goes round a star other than the Sun.
terms.example: TRAPPIST-1 has seven exoplanets going round it.
terms.art: A small red star with seven planets in a row around it.

terms.meaning: When a planet passes between us and its star, and blocks a tiny part of the star's light.
terms.example: Astronomers find many exoplanets by noticing that a star dims a tiny bit every few days.
terms.art: A star with a small planet crossing in front of it, and a graph below showing a small dip.

terms.meaning: A small, dim, cool star. Red dwarfs are the most common stars in our galaxy.
terms.example: TRAPPIST-1 is a red dwarf only a little bigger than Jupiter.
terms.art: A small dim red star next to a large bright yellow Sun for comparison.

terms.meaning: A chain of estimates, started by Frank Drake in 1961, for how many civilisations there might be in our galaxy who could send signals.
terms.example: The Drake equation multiplies the number of stars by the share with planets, the share of those with life, and so on.
terms.art: A line of boxes joined by multiplication signs, getting smaller from left to right.

terms.meaning: A gas made of carbon and hydrogen. On Earth, most methane is made by living things such as microbes in cattle stomachs and in wet paddy fields.
terms.example: Titan has lakes of liquid methane, and Mars has a tiny, puzzling amount of methane in its air.
terms.art: A methane molecule drawn as a ball with four smaller balls around it.

terms.meaning: A gas made of carbon and oxygen. Living things breathe it out, and plants take it in. Venus and Mars have air that is mostly carbon dioxide.
terms.example: Your breath holds about a hundred times more carbon dioxide than the air you breathed in.
terms.art: A carbon dioxide molecule with one large ball in the middle and two balls on either side.

terms.meaning: A tiny living thing, a kind of fungus, that is one cell. Yeast eats sugar and makes carbon dioxide gas. Bakers use yeast to make bread rise.
terms.example: In idli and dosa batter, yeast and bacteria make gas, so the batter swells and gets bubbles.
terms.art: Many tiny round yeast cells, some with a small bud, with gas bubbles around them.

terms.meaning: A molecule built on a framework of carbon atoms, like the molecules that living things are made of. Organic does not mean alive, because non-living chemistry can make them too.
terms.example: Curiosity, a rover on Mars, found organic molecules in an old rock.
terms.art: A chain of carbon balls with smaller balls attached.

terms.meaning: The distance that light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Astronomers use it to measure distances between stars.
terms.example: TRAPPIST-1 is about 40 light-years away, so the light we see from it today left the star about 40 years ago.
terms.art: A beam of light crossing a line marked with years from one star to another.

terms.meaning: A jet of gas, water or ice that shoots out of a world into space.
terms.example: Enceladus has plumes that spray out of cracks near its south pole.
terms.art: A small icy moon with long white jets spraying from cracks near the bottom.

explanations.concept: A habitable zone depends on the star
explanations.context: In the first Life beyond Earth unit you learned that life needs liquid water. This card asks where a planet must be to have liquid water on its surface.
explanations.definition: The habitable zone is the ring of distances from a star where a planet could be warm enough to have liquid water on its surface. A bright star has a zone far out, and a dim star has a zone close in.
explanations.description: A planet gets warmer the closer it is to its star, because the light spreads out as it travels. If a planet is too close, its water boils off. If it is too far, its water freezes. Between the two is the habitable zone, sometimes called the Goldilocks zone, after a story of porridge that was not too hot and not too cold. Different stars have different zones. The Sun is bright, so its zone lies at about the distance of Earth. A red dwarf like TRAPPIST-1 is small and dim, so its zone is very close in, even closer than Mercury is to the Sun. Being inside the zone does not by itself make a world a place where life could live. It only means that liquid water on the surface is possible, if the world also has air and the right amount of water.
examples: Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun, in the middle of the Sun's zone.
Venus is about 108 million kilometres from the Sun, and is far too hot.
TRAPPIST-1's habitable zone is only a few million kilometres from the star.
explanations.art: Two stars, a big yellow Sun with a distant green ring and a small red dwarf with a green ring very close in, with planets placed in the rings.

explanations.concept: More than distance: air, size and a magnetic field
explanations.context: The habitable zone is about distance. This card shows that distance is not enough, using our two neighbours Venus and Mars.
explanations.definition: A world's temperature depends on its distance from the star, and also on its atmosphere, its size and its magnetic field.
explanations.description: Venus is only a little closer to the Sun than Earth, but it is about 460 degrees Celsius on the surface, hot enough to melt lead. The reason is its air. Venus has a very thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide, and that gas holds back heat. This is called the greenhouse effect. Mars is the opposite. It is smaller than Earth, so its gravity is weaker, and it has lost most of its air. Its air is now less than a hundredth as thick as ours, and the average temperature is about minus 60 degrees. Scientists think Mars lost its global magnetic field long ago. That let the solar wind, a stream of fast particles from the Sun, strip away much of its air. Earth has a thick enough atmosphere and a magnetic field, which helps to keep its water.
examples: Venus is hotter than Mercury, though Mercury is much closer to the Sun, because of Venus's thick air.
Mars's thin air cannot hold heat or water on its surface, so water there is mostly ice.
Earth's magnetic field bends away fast particles from the Sun, which helps to keep our air.
explanations.art: Three planets in a row: Venus with a thick yellow atmosphere, Earth with a thin blue atmosphere and a magnetic field, and Mars with almost no atmosphere.

explanations.context: In the first Life beyond Earth unit you met microbes at deep-sea vents. This card says how they get their energy in the dark, because it changes where scientists look.
explanations.definition: Some bacteria make food from chemicals, not from sunlight. This is called chemosynthesis. It lets life live in places with no light.
explanations.description: Plants make food using sunlight. In 1977, scientists in the submarine Alvin found a crowd of animals around hot vents on the dark sea floor, far below any sunlight. There were giant tube worms, clams and crabs. Their food chain starts with bacteria. The bacteria take hydrogen sulfide, a gas that comes out of the vent, and join it with oxygen from the sea water. The chemical reaction gives out energy, which the bacteria use to make food. A giant tube worm has no mouth and no stomach. Instead, bacteria live inside her body and feed her. So a living world needs an energy supply, but the energy does not have to be light. This means that life could live in the dark oceans under the ice of Europa and Enceladus, if hot rock below gives them chemicals.
examples: A giant tube worm lives on sugars made by the bacteria inside her body.
Hydrothermal vents were found on the sea floor near the Galapagos Islands in 1977.
Microbes in the dark rocks deep under the ground also live on chemicals, with no light.
explanations.art: A hot vent on the dark sea floor with a group of tube worms, and a cut-open worm showing bacteria inside her body.

explanations.concept: Enceladus and Europa: oceans under the ice
explanations.context: These two icy moons are the best places in the solar system to look for life. This card says what spacecraft have found, and what is still guesswork.
explanations.definition: Enceladus and Europa very probably hold salty oceans under their ice. Spacecraft have found chemicals in the plumes of Enceladus that life could use, but nobody has found life.
explanations.description: The Cassini spacecraft flew through the plumes of Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, many times. It found water, salt and some organic molecules in the spray. In 2017 scientists reported that it also found hydrogen, a gas that could be food for microbes at hot vents on the moon's sea floor. In 2023 other scientists reported that ice grains in the spray contained phosphates, which life needs to build DNA. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, is bigger, and its ocean may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans. The Europa Clipper spacecraft was launched in 2024 to study the moon. Both moons are warmed inside by the pull of their planet, which squeezes them a little more and a little less as they go round. These are strong clues, but not proof of life.
examples: Cassini flew through Enceladus's plumes and tested the spray for salt, hydrogen and organic molecules.
Europa Clipper is planned to reach Jupiter in 2030 and fly past Europa many times.
Saturn's pull squeezes Enceladus a little more and a little less as it goes round, which warms the moon inside.
explanations.art: Enceladus with white jets spraying from its south pole, a cutaway showing a hidden ocean and a hot rocky core.

explanations.concept: Mars: old lakes, strange rocks and a puzzling gas
explanations.context: Mars is the planet we have studied most closely for signs of life. This card says what has been found and what scientists disagree about.
explanations.description: Mars has dry river valleys and old lake beds, so it once had liquid water. In 2018, NASA's Curiosity rover reported organic molecules in an old rock. These molecules are the kind that life is built from, but non-living chemistry can make them too. Curiosity also measured a very small amount of methane in the air, which seemed to go up and down with the seasons. On Earth most methane is made by life, but it can also be made by rocks. Another spacecraft later found much less methane. In 2024, the Perseverance rover studied a rock named Cheyava Falls, with small spots like a leopard's. NASA said this was a possible sign of past life, but the spots may also have formed without life. Samples have been collected, but they are still on Mars.
examples: Perseverance has been collecting rock samples from Jezero crater, an old lake bed, since 2021.
Curiosity found organic molecules in an old rock in Gale crater, another ancient lake.
Methane on Mars was reported to rise and fall with the seasons, but another spacecraft found very little.
explanations.art: A rover on the red surface of Mars, drilling into a rock with small pale spots, and a dry river valley behind.

perspectives.who: Some scientists on the Perseverance team
perspectives.explanation: The leopard spots on Cheyava Falls look like marks made by microbes on Earth. This is a possible sign of past life, and the samples should be brought to Earth.
The same spots can form without life, from chemical reactions in the mud. Without a sample in a lab here, we cannot be sure.
Everyone agrees the rock is interesting. Bringing the sample back to labs on Earth would give a much better test, but it is not certain that such a mission will happen.

explanations.concept: Titan: a world with a different kind of liquid
explanations.context: Most searches for life look for liquid water. This card is about a moon that has liquid, but not water, on its surface.
explanations.definition: Titan, a moon of Saturn, has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane on its surface, and a thick nitrogen atmosphere. It is too cold for water to be liquid there.
explanations.description: Titan is the only moon in our solar system with a thick atmosphere. It is about minus 179 degrees on the surface. In such cold, water is ice, and the ice is as hard as rock. But methane and ethane, which are gases on Earth, are liquid there. Rain falls, rivers run and lakes fill. In 2005 the Huygens probe landed on Titan. NASA plans to send a flying lander, called Dragonfly, in the late 2020s. Some scientists wonder whether a kind of life could use methane as its liquid instead of water. Nobody has found such life, and nobody knows if it could exist. Under the ice, Titan may also have a layer of liquid water. Titan shows us that life as we know it may not be the only kind to look for.
examples: Rivers of liquid methane have carved valleys on Titan, like rivers of water on Earth.
The Huygens probe sent back pictures from Titan's surface in 2005.
Dragonfly is a planned drone-like lander that will fly from place to place on Titan.
explanations.art: A dim orange-hazed moon with a dark lake of methane on its surface and a small drone-like lander flying above the shore.

explanations.concept: Biosignatures: signs of life in the air of a world
explanations.context: Scientists cannot visit a faraway planet. This card says how a planet's air can show that something lives there.
explanations.definition: A biosignature is a sign that life has been there. The best-known one is a mix of gases in a planet's air that would not last together unless living things kept making them.
explanations.description: Earth's air is about one fifth oxygen and has a little methane. Oxygen and methane react with each other, and in a few years they would disappear. They are still there because living things such as plants, algae and microbes keep making them. In 1965 the scientist James Lovelock pointed out that this is how an observer could tell that Earth has life without landing. If a world's air holds gases that react with each other but never run out, something is probably refilling them. This is called an atmosphere out of balance. Yeast in a bottle show the same idea. The yeast keep making carbon dioxide from the sugar, and the balloon stays swollen.
examples: Without plants and microbes, the oxygen in Earth's air would be used up in a short time, compared with the age of the Earth.
Most of the methane in Earth's air is made by living things such as microbes in wet rice fields and in the stomachs of cattle.
A bottle of yeast and sugar swells a balloon, but a bottle of sugar alone does not.
explanations.art: Earth with arrows labelled oxygen and methane being refilled by trees, microbes and cattle, and a telescope reading its air.

explanations.concept: False alarms: when a gas is not a sign of life
explanations.context: A gas that looks like a sign of life can sometimes be made by non-living chemistry. This card shows why scientists argue about the claims they have heard.
explanations.description: Oxygen on its own is not proof of life. On some planets, strong light from a star can split water or carbon dioxide and make oxygen with no living thing involved. In 2020, scientists reported a gas called phosphine in the clouds of Venus. On Earth phosphine is made mostly by microbes. Other teams looked again and found much less, or none. In 2023, a team led by Nikku Madhusudhan, an astrophysicist born in India who works in Cambridge, used the James Webb Space Telescope to study a planet called K2-18 b, about 120 light-years away. They found methane and carbon dioxide. There was also a hint of dimethyl sulfide, a gas that on Earth is made mostly by tiny sea plankton. Other teams re-examined the data and did not agree that the hint was real.
examples: A hot planet could make oxygen by splitting water in its air, with no life.
The Venus phosphine claim of 2020 was questioned by other teams who looked at the same data.
The K2-18 b hint of dimethyl sulfide is not accepted by all astronomers.
explanations.art: A planet with a gas label, a question mark, and two scientists on either side of a graph pointing at different lines.

perspectives.who: Scientists who reported the K2-18 b hint
perspectives.explanation: A sign of a gas that life makes on Earth is worth following up. More observations with the James Webb Space Telescope could make it clearer.

perspectives.who: Other scientists who re-examined the data
perspectives.explanation: The hint is weak and may be noise. Other chemistry could make the gases, and nobody is even sure what kind of planet it is.
One gas will never be enough. A claim of life needs several signs that fit together, repeated by different teams, and no better non-living explanation.

explanations.concept: How we find planets and read their air
explanations.context: Planets around other stars are many light-years away. This card says how astronomers find them at all and how they read their air.
explanations.definition: Astronomers find many exoplanets by the tiny dip in a star's light when a planet passes in front, called a transit. They read a planet's air from the colours missing in the starlight that passes through it.
explanations.description: A planet is far too faint to see next to its bright star. But when it crosses in front of the star, the starlight dims a tiny bit. Jupiter would block about 1 part in 100 of the Sun's light, and Earth only about 1 part in 10,000. If the dip repeats, the planet is real, and the time between dips is the length of its year. When the planet is in front, a little starlight also passes through the thin ring of its air. Each gas takes away its own colours from the light. So the spectrum, the starlight spread into a rainbow, has dark gaps that show which gases are there. In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope found carbon dioxide in the air of a hot gas planet named WASP-39 b. In 2018, scientists at the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad reported the first planet found from India, using a telescope at Mount Abu.
examples: A star that dims by 1 part in 100 every 6 days has a big planet with a 6-day year.
Kepler, a space telescope launched in 2009, found thousands of planets with the transit method.
Each gas in a planet's air takes away its own set of colours from the starlight.
explanations.art: A star with a planet crossing in front of it, a graph of brightness showing a dip, and a rainbow strip with dark gaps for each gas.

explanations.concept: TRAPPIST-1: seven worlds around a red dwarf
explanations.context: This card brings the ideas together in one real planetary system, about 40 light-years from us.
explanations.definition: TRAPPIST-1 is a small red dwarf star with seven Earth-sized planets going round it. Three of them lie in the habitable zone.
explanations.description: In 2017, astronomers led by Michael Gillon in Belgium reported seven planets going round TRAPPIST-1, a dim red star about 40 light-years from Earth. The star is only a little bigger than Jupiter, and all seven planets orbit closer to it than Mercury does to our Sun. Their years last only from 1.5 to about 19 days. Planets e, f and g are often named as lying in the habitable zone. But a red dwarf sends out strong flares, and the planets are probably locked so that one side always faces the star. In 2023 the James Webb Space Telescope looked at the two inner planets and reported that they seem to have no thick atmosphere. Nobody yet knows if any of the outer planets has air, or water. This is a good place to test the methods in this unit.
examples: One of the TRAPPIST-1 planets is so close to the star that its year lasts less than two Earth days.
The James Webb Space Telescope has begun to study the air of the TRAPPIST-1 planets.
A planet locked to its star has one side in permanent day and one side in permanent night.
explanations.art: A small dim red star at the left with seven planets of different colours in a line to the right, with three of them inside a green zone.

explanations.concept: The Drake equation: a chain of guesses
explanations.context: Scientists cannot count how many civilisations there are. This card says how they organise what they do and do not know.
explanations.definition: The Drake equation multiplies a chain of numbers to estimate how many civilisations in our galaxy might send signals. Some numbers are known and some are guesses, so the answer depends mostly on the guesses.
explanations.description: In 1961, the astronomer Frank Drake wrote a list of the numbers that decide how many civilisations we might hear from. The first numbers are the number of stars in the galaxy, which is at least 100 billion, and the share of stars that have planets, which astronomers now think is most of them. After that, the numbers become guesses. What share of habitable planets get life? What share of life becomes intelligent? How long does a civilisation last and send signals? If you guess that each step is easy, you might get millions of civilisations. If you guess that one step is very rare, you might get only one, which is us. The equation does not tell us the answer. It tells us which numbers we most need to find out, such as how often life begins.
examples: Astronomers can now count planets, so one early number of the chain is no longer a guess.
Nobody knows how often life begins when conditions are right, because we have only one example.
Guessing that one step is very rare can reduce the answer from millions of civilisations to almost none.
explanations.art: A funnel with a very large number of stars at the top, and smaller and smaller numbers at each step down to a few at the bottom.

explanations.context: To look for life we must know what we are looking for. This card shows why that is harder than it sounds.
explanations.description: A working definition used by NASA is that life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. That means it keeps itself going using energy, and it passes on changes so that its kind can adapt over many generations. By this idea, yeast, a tardigrade and a banyan tree are alive. A fire grows and uses fuel, but does not pass on a code, so it is not alive. A virus carries a code and evolves, but cannot make more of itself without a host cell, so many scientists say a virus is on the edge of being alive. A crystal grows too, but does not use energy to keep itself going. Any definition built from life on Earth may miss life that works in another way, and scientists keep debating it.
examples: A fire uses fuel and grows, but does not copy a code, so it is not usually called alive.
A virus carries a code and evolves, but needs a host cell to make more virus.
A seed can sit for years doing almost nothing and still be alive.
explanations.art: A row of five things, a yeast cell, a flame, a virus, a crystal and a seed, with a question mark under each.

perspectives.who: Scientists who use the NASA definition
perspectives.explanation: Life is a chemical system that keeps itself going and can evolve. It is a useful working idea for deciding what to look for.

perspectives.who: Scientists who think any definition is too narrow
perspectives.explanation: We have only one example of life. A definition built from it may leave out forms of life that work in other ways.
There is no agreed answer. Most scientists work with a flexible idea and judge each case by how many of the signs of life it shows.

explanations.context: Everything so far looks for life of any kind. This card is about listening for a signal from a civilisation that might send one on purpose.
explanations.definition: SETI, the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, uses radio telescopes to listen for signals that natural things could not make. No such signal has been confirmed.
explanations.description: A civilisation that wanted to be noticed could send a radio signal. Radio waves cross space quickly and are easy to receive. SETI scientists such as Jill Tarter have listened to many stars for decades. They look for a signal that is very narrow, in a single pitch, because nature rarely makes such a signal. On 15 August 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope in Ohio, in the United States, recorded a strong narrow signal that lasted for 72 seconds. Jerry Ehman, who found it in the printout, wrote Wow! next to it. It has never been heard again, and nobody knows what made it. Signals take time. A message from a star 40 light-years away would take 40 years to arrive.
examples: The Wow! signal of 1977 was strong and narrow but never repeated.
Most strange signals turn out to come from satellites, aircraft or machines on Earth.
A reply to a message sent to a star 40 light-years away would take at least 80 years to come back.
explanations.art: A large radio telescope dish pointed at the night sky, and a printout showing a row of letters and numbers with Wow! written in red pen next to one line.

agreed.text: A planet's temperature depends on its air as well as its distance from the star.
agreed.evidence: Venus is about 460 degrees Celsius, hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun. Space probes measured both, and the cause is the thick carbon dioxide air of Venus.

agreed.text: Europa and Enceladus very probably have salty oceans of liquid water under their ice.
agreed.evidence: The Cassini spacecraft flew through spray from Enceladus and found salt and water. Magnetic measurements by the Galileo spacecraft fit a salty ocean on Europa.

agreed.text: Some living things get their energy from chemicals, not from sunlight.
agreed.evidence: In 1977 scientists found animals around hot vents on the dark sea floor. Their food starts with bacteria that make food from hydrogen sulfide.
In 2018 the Curiosity rover reported organic molecules in an old rock. Organic molecules can also be made without life, so this does not show life.

agreed.text: There are thousands of planets going round other stars.
agreed.evidence: More than 5,000 exoplanets have been confirmed, found by the dip of starlight in a transit and by the tiny wobble they cause in their stars.

agreed.text: A gas in a planet's air can be read from its starlight.
agreed.evidence: In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope found carbon dioxide in the air of the planet WASP-39 b, many light-years away, from the colours missing in the starlight.

agreed.text: No life has been found anywhere except on Earth.
agreed.evidence: Every claim so far, from canals on Mars to gas on Venus, has had another explanation that most scientists find more likely.

challenging.claim: Life can only live in the habitable zone, at the right distance from a star.
challenging.who: A natural guess, from the Goldilocks idea.
challenging.for: Liquid water on a surface needs the right warmth, and a planet too near or too far loses it.
challenging.against: Europa and Enceladus are far outside the Sun's zone, yet probably have oceans, because their planet's pull warms them inside. Life might live under ice, far from any star's warmth.
challenging.context: This card looks at whether the habitable zone is the only place where life can live.

challenging.claim: If a planet's air has oxygen, it must have life.
challenging.who: Many people, and some early scientific papers.
challenging.for: On Earth, nearly all oxygen comes from plants, algae and microbes.
challenging.against: On some planets, strong starlight can split water or carbon dioxide and make oxygen with no life. A gas alone is not enough. Scientists look for several signs that fit together.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common idea about oxygen as a sign of life.

challenging.claim: The 2024 leopard-spot rock on Mars shows that microbes once lived there.
challenging.for: The spots look like marks made by microbes in rocks on Earth, and NASA called them a possible biosignature.
challenging.against: The same spots can form from chemistry alone. Scientists say they need to study the sample in laboratories on Earth, and the plan to bring it back is uncertain.
challenging.context: This card looks at a claim about a rock on Mars.

challenging.claim: The methane on Mars is made by microbes.
challenging.who: Some scientists, after the Curiosity rover measured methane from 2013 to 2019.
challenging.for: On Earth most methane is made by life, and Curiosity saw it rise and fall with the seasons.
challenging.against: Rocks can make methane without life, and another spacecraft later measured much less. The amount is tiny and its source is unknown.
challenging.context: This card looks at where Mars's methane comes from.

challenging.claim: A hint of dimethyl sulfide on the planet K2-18 b means it has life.
challenging.who: Reports by a team led by Nikku Madhusudhan, in 2023 and 2025.
challenging.for: On Earth, dimethyl sulfide is made mostly by sea plankton, and the team saw a hint of it.
challenging.against: Other teams looked at the data again and found the hint was weak or not there. Non-living chemistry may also make it, and the planet itself is not well understood.
challenging.context: This card looks at a claim about life on a planet outside our solar system.

challenging.claim: The Viking landers found life on Mars in 1976.
challenging.who: Gilbert Levin, who designed one of the Viking tests, and a few others.
challenging.for: A test that fed nutrients to Martian soil gave off gas, as living microbes would.
challenging.against: Another Viking instrument found no organic molecules. Later missions found chemicals in Martian soil that could explain the gas without life. Most scientists do not accept the claim.
challenging.context: This card looks at an early claim about life on Mars.

challenging.claim: All life must use liquid water.
challenging.who: Most biologists, because all known life does.
challenging.for: Every living thing found so far needs liquid water to carry out the reactions of life.
challenging.against: We have only one kind of life to study. Some scientists ask whether another liquid, like the methane on Titan, could take the place of water. Nobody has found such life.
challenging.context: This card looks at whether life must use water.

challenging.claim: If aliens existed, we would have heard from them by now.
challenging.who: Enrico Fermi, who asked this question in 1950, and many who repeat it.
challenging.for: The galaxy is old and has billions of stars, so a civilisation has had a long time to spread or send signals.
challenging.against: We have listened to a tiny part of the sky and a tiny set of signal types for a short time. Signals take years to cross space, and a civilisation may not last long or may not send any.
challenging.context: This card looks at the question of why we have not heard from anyone.

big_questions.q: You cannot see yeast, but you can see a balloon swell. Is a balloon good evidence of life?
big_questions.hint: Think about what else could swell a balloon, and how you could test it.

big_questions.q: Venus is hotter than Mercury, though Mercury is closer to the Sun. What does this tell you about planets?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the air does to heat.

big_questions.q: Why can bacteria live on chemicals in the dark, and a plant cannot?
big_questions.hint: Think about where each gets its energy.

big_questions.q: A cup of milk with a spoon of curd does not set in a fridge, but sets later when moved somewhere warm. Were the curd bacteria dead or asleep, and how could you tell?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you saw when you moved it somewhere warm.

big_questions.q: If we find a gas that could be a sign of life, how much proof is enough to say there is life?
big_questions.hint: Think about who should check the claim, and what would change your mind.

big_questions.q: Many news stories say 'signs of life found on another planet'. Who should we trust, and how can a child check?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between what was observed and what was guessed.

big_questions.q: Is it better to spend money on looking for life in space, or on caring for life on Earth?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each could teach us, and whether the two can help each other.

big_questions.q: If we found a living microbe on Mars, would that change how you feel about Earth?
big_questions.hint: Think about what it would mean if life started more than once.

story.title: The Batter on the Balcony
story.note: A made-up story. The family, the kitchen and the winter morning in Bengaluru are imagined. The science is real. Idli batter rises when yeast and bacteria make gas, cold slows them down, and heat that is too great kills them.
text: It was the coldest week in Bengaluru, and the idli batter had not risen.
Thenmozhi lifted the lid of the steel container on the balcony. Last night the batter had been smooth and white. This morning it was smooth and white. It lay in the container like a flat pond.
'It's dead,' said her brother Hari. He was seven, and he liked announcing things. 'The batter has died. No idli.'
Their grandmother, Paati, had come from Madurai for the week, because Amma was away at a conference. She leaned over the container and sniffed it. Then she shook her head slowly.
'Not dead,' said Paati. 'Asleep. The little ones who make the batter rise do not like cold. It was twelve degrees last night.'
'What little ones?' said Hari.
'The yeast, and the bacteria,' said Paati. 'They are too small to see, but they are in every spoon.'
Thenmozhi frowned. 'How do you know they are even alive, if we cannot see them?'

Paati pointed at the spoon in the container. 'When they are awake, three things happen. The batter swells, and it lifts the lid. Tiny bubbles come up through it. And the smell turns a little sour. You never see them. You see what they do to the air.'

Thenmozhi sat down on the floor with a bump. She had read about Mars the night before. 'Paati, that is how scientists look for life on other planets! They cannot see any creature on a planet that far away. They look at the gases.'
'Then you are a scientist,' said Paati, and her eyes were bright. 'Find me the planet where my little ones can live.'

So they held a search. Thenmozhi spooned a little batter into four small steel katoris, and covered each one. She put one on the cold balcony and called it Mars. She put one on the shelf above the fridge, where the back of the machine gave a gentle warmth. She put one inside the oven, which was switched off, with just the little oven light on. And Hari, grinning, put one on top of the hot water geyser.
'That is Venus,' he said. 'The hot planet.'
'Venus will not work,' said Paati. 'But let him. Nothing teaches like a test that fails.'
They waited all afternoon. Every hour, Thenmozhi lifted each lid and looked.

By evening, Mars had not changed at all. It was flat and cold. Venus on the geyser was flat as well, and it smelled like cooked flour. The cup above the fridge had a few bubbles. But the cup in the oven, with its small light, had risen into a soft white dome. Its lid sat crooked, pushed up by the gas. When Thenmozhi smelled it, it was sour and sweet at once.
'That one is awake,' said Hari. 'That is the Earth cup.'
'And Venus is dead,' said Thenmozhi. 'The heat was too much for the little ones.'
'But look at Mars,' said Paati. 'Move that cup in with Earth.'
Thenmozhi carried the cold katori into the warm oven. She had to wait all night. In the morning, Mars had a few bubbles, and by lunchtime it had a small dome of its own.
'It was only asleep!' said Hari.
Thenmozhi nodded slowly. 'Cold is a pause,' she said. 'Heat that is too great is the end. Venus never woke up.'

Paati poured the good batter into the idli plates, and the kitchen filled with steam. Hari looked at the container with the dome of batter in it. 'If a spaceship came and looked at our kitchen from far away,' he said, 'how would the visitors know there was life in there?'
'They could not see the yeast,' said Thenmozhi. 'But they could see the gas.'
story.epiphany: We cannot see tiny living things from far away, but we can see what they do to their surroundings. A lifted lid, a swollen balloon, or a gas that nothing else explains is a sign that something alive is there.
ask: Why can a swelling balloon or a lifted lid show that tiny living things are present, though you cannot see them?
The batter on the hot geyser never rose, but the batter from the cold balcony rose later in the warm oven. Why?
How is looking at a planet's air like looking at the batter's lid?
What other explanation could there be for bubbles, besides living things?

A grandmother pointing at a lid slightly lifted on a container of batter, while her granddaughter looks closely.
Four small steel katoris in a row with lids: one on a cold balcony, one above a fridge, one inside an oven with the light on, and one on top of a geyser.

games.title: Biosignature Detectives: is it a sign of life?
games.context: This is a game about reading clues from far away. Each card shows something a scientist might find in a far-off planet's air or on a moon. You decide if it is a strong hint of life, not a sign of life, or too early to tell.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with three tokens in front of each player: strong hint, not a sign, can't tell.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One player reading a card aloud about a bottle with a swollen balloon, while the others put down tokens face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token and puts it face down.

setup.art: Tokens turned over together and the reader showing the back of the card with the answer and reason.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. Then the reader reads the back.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a clue on the front, and what it means on the back

items.f: A planet's air has about one fifth oxygen and a little methane, and both keep being refilled.
items.b: Strong hint of life. Oxygen and methane react and would vanish. Something keeps making both. This is Earth's air.

items.f: A sealed bottle of sugar water and yeast has a balloon on top. The balloon swells.
items.b: Strong hint of life. Yeast eat sugar and give out carbon dioxide, so something in the bottle is making gas.

items.f: Three different telescopes find oxygen, methane and dimethyl sulfide in one planet's air.
items.b: Strong hint of life. Several signs fit together and were seen by more than one team. It would still need checking.

items.f: A planet's air has carbon dioxide that falls every spring and rises every autumn, and oxygen that stays high.
items.b: Strong hint of life. On Earth, plants take in carbon dioxide in the growing season and release it later.

items.f: A sealed jar of sprouting moong seeds has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide after two days.
items.b: Strong hint of life. Sprouting seeds breathe. They use oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.

items.f: Suppose the spray from an icy moon holds long chains of organic molecules in a pattern like the ones in living cells.
items.b: Strong hint of life. Non-living chemistry rarely makes such patterns. Other teams would still need to check it.

items.f: The air of a world is thick carbon dioxide, with acid clouds, and the surface is 460 degrees.
items.b: Not a sign of life. The gases are in balance, and the heat is far too great. This is Venus.

items.f: A hot planet very close to its star has a lot of oxygen. The strong starlight splits its water.
items.b: Not a sign of life. Strong light can split water and make oxygen without life. This is a false alarm.

items.f: A planet's air is only nitrogen and a little argon. Nothing in it reacts with anything else.
items.b: Not a sign of life. Everything is in balance, and nothing seems to need refilling.

items.f: A sealed bottle of sugar water has no yeast, and the balloon stays flat.
items.b: Not a sign of life. Nothing is making gas.

items.f: In 1976 a photograph of Mars showed a hill that looked like a face.
items.b: Not a sign of life. Shapes can trick us. Later, sharper pictures showed an ordinary hill.

items.f: A dry rock on the Moon has a smooth round pit.
items.b: Not a sign of life. Space rocks hit the Moon and dig pits like this. The pit is a crater.

items.f: A very small amount of methane on Mars rises and falls with the seasons.
items.b: Can't tell yet. Rocks can make methane, and so can life. Scientists disagree.

items.f: The spray from Enceladus holds water, salt, hydrogen and organic molecules.
items.b: Can't tell yet. This is good food for microbes, but chemistry can make it without life.

items.f: One team sees a hint of dimethyl sulfide on a far planet called K2-18 b. Others do not see it.
items.b: Can't tell yet. On Earth plankton make this gas, but the hint is weak, and teams disagree.

items.f: Titan, a moon of Saturn, has lakes of liquid methane and a thick orange haze.
items.b: Can't tell yet. The chemistry is strange and interesting, but no sign of life has been found.

items.f: On 15 August 1977 a radio telescope heard a strong, narrow signal for 72 seconds, and never heard it again.
items.b: Can't tell yet. This is the Wow! signal. It never repeated, so nobody can check it.

items.f: A rock on Mars named Cheyava Falls has small spots like a leopard's.
items.b: Can't tell yet. The spots may be a sign of past life, but they can also form without life.

items.f: Scientists reported phosphine, a gas made mostly by life on Earth, in the clouds of Venus.
items.b: Can't tell yet. Other teams found much less or none, so the claim is not accepted.

items.f: An old rock on Mars holds organic molecules.
items.b: Can't tell yet. Organic molecules are the building blocks of life, but non-living chemistry makes them too.

printables.title: 3 answer tokens to cut out for each player
Score sheet
items: Good reason or a second clue to look for (1 more point)

rules: Each player gets three tokens: Strong hint of life, Not a sign of life, and Can't tell yet. Shuffle the cards into a pile, clue side up.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Everyone else puts one token face down. Then everyone turns their token over together.
Each player says why they chose that token. A good reason says what clue matters, or what other explanation could fool us.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back aloud. A right answer scores 1 point. A good reason, or naming a second clue that would help, scores 1 more point.
Pass the reader job to the next player. Play until the pile runs out. The most points wins. In a tie, everyone wins.
Playing alone: take the top card, put a token on it, then check the back. Score 1 for each right answer out of 20, and try to beat your score another day.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Give each player three tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Read the three tokens aloud.
flow.say: Scientists hunt for life on faraway worlds by reading clues. Some clues are strong hints of life. Some are not signs of life at all. For some, it is too early to tell. You must choose, and say why.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. The three answers are: strong hint of life, not a sign of life, and can't tell yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Biosignature Detectives game. You set up the cards and tokens.

flow.do: Play the two bottle cards face up together. Talk about each one. Ask what else could make a balloon swell.
flow.say: A bottle of sugar water and yeast has a balloon that swells. Is that a strong hint of life, not a sign of life, or can't tell yet? A bottle of sugar water with no yeast has a flat balloon. What is the difference?
flow.kid: Read the two bottle cards. Pick a token for each. Say why.

check.q: A balloon on a bottle of sugar water and yeast swells. Why is that a strong hint of life?
options: Something is giving out gas, and the bottle without yeast gave out none
Balloons always swell on bottles
The balloon is made of living material
check.why: A fair comparison is the key. The same bottle without yeast stayed flat, so the yeast made the difference. Picking 'balloons always swell' misses the flat balloon on the bottle with no yeast.

flow.context: In this step, you practise with the two bottle cards before the real game.

flow.do: Play the game as the rules say. Keep a pile of the cards you got wrong, to look at again at the end.
flow.say: Reader, read the clue. Everyone, put down a token face down. Turn them over together. Now tell us why. Then the reader reads the back.
flow.kid: Read a card. Put down a token. Turn it over. Say why.

ask.q: A planet's air has oxygen in it. Why is that not enough to say there is life?
good: Strong starlight can make oxygen from water, with no life.
We need more than one sign.
Other teams need to check.

flow.parent: The best reasons name an outside explanation that could fool us, such as chemistry or strong light. The 'can't tell yet' answer is not a weak answer. It is the honest one when the evidence is thin.
flow.context: In this step, you play the game and learn to weigh clues.

flow.do: Spread out the cards that were hard. Sort all 20 cards into the three groups. Ask what the strong hints have in common.
flow.say: Let's sort all the cards into three piles. What do the strong hints have in common? What does it take to move a card from can't tell yet into a strong hint?
flow.kid: Sort all the cards into 3 piles. What do the strong hints share?
flow.think: If one team found a hint of life and nobody else could repeat it, how many other clues would you want?
flow.context: In this step, you sort the cards and think about what makes a clue strong.

games.title: Goldilocks Line-Up: too hot, just right or too cold?
games.context: This is a game about the habitable zone. Each card shows a world and how far it is from its star. You put each one in a box: too hot, just right, or too cold. The same distance can give very different answers around different stars.

setup.art: Two paper boards on a table, one for the Sun and one for TRAPPIST-1, each with three boxes labelled too hot, just right and too cold.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two boards, one for the Sun and one for TRAPPIST-1.

setup.art: A child holding a planet card that says Earth, 150 million kilometres from the Sun, over the middle box.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Guess which box it goes in.

setup.art: The card turned over to show the answer and a short reason.
setup.caption: 3. Place the card in the box. Turn it over to check.

printables.title: 2 boards: one for the Sun and one for TRAPPIST-1, each with three boxes
items: Board for the Sun: three boxes in a row, labelled Too hot, Just right and Too cold.
Board for TRAPPIST-1: three boxes in a row, labelled Too hot, Just right and Too cold.

printables.title: 14 two-sided cards: a world and its distance on the front, and the answer on the back

items.f: Around the Sun. Mercury, 58 million kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: Too hot. Mercury is so close that its sunny side is hot enough to melt lead.

items.f: Around the Sun. Venus, 108 million kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: Too hot. Venus is near the hot inner edge, and its thick carbon dioxide air makes it about 460 degrees.

items.f: Around the Sun. Earth, 150 million kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: Just right. Earth has liquid water on its surface, thanks to its distance and its air.

items.f: Around the Sun. Mars, 228 million kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: Too cold. Mars is near the cold outer edge, and it is small and has lost most of its air, so water there is mostly ice.

items.f: Around the Sun. Jupiter, 778 million kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: Too cold. Jupiter is far outside the zone, and water at its cloud tops is frozen. Its moons may be warmed from inside.

items.f: Around the Sun. Neptune, about 4,500 million kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: Too cold. Sunlight there is about 900 times weaker than on Earth.

items.f: Around the Sun. An imaginary planet, 5 million kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: Too hot. This is far closer than Mercury, and it would be scorched.

items.f: Around TRAPPIST-1. Planet b, about 1.7 million kilometres from the star.
items.b: Too hot. It is the closest, and very likely scorched.

items.f: Around TRAPPIST-1. Planet d, about 3.3 million kilometres from the star.
items.b: Too hot, probably. It is at the hot inner edge, and scientists are not sure.

items.f: Around TRAPPIST-1. Planet e, about 4.4 million kilometres from the star.
items.b: Just right, possibly. It is in the zone, but it may have no air, and we do not know.

items.f: Around TRAPPIST-1. Planet f, about 5.8 million kilometres from the star.
items.b: Just right, possibly. It is in the zone. Whether it has water or air is unknown.

items.f: Around TRAPPIST-1. Planet g, about 7.0 million kilometres from the star.
items.b: Just right, possibly. This planet is about as near its star as the imaginary planet 5 million kilometres from the Sun, but its star is much dimmer.

items.f: Around TRAPPIST-1. Planet h, about 9.3 million kilometres from the star.
items.b: Too cold, probably. It is at the cold outer edge, and scientists are not sure.

items.f: Around TRAPPIST-1. An imaginary planet, 150 million kilometres from the star.
items.b: Too cold. The star is so dim that a planet at Earth's distance would be far too cold.

rules: Lay out the two boards. Shuffle the cards and make a pile, front side up.
The reader takes a card and reads it aloud, saying which star and how far.
Everyone puts their finger on the box they choose. Then they say why.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer. A right box scores 1 point. If you can say why, you score 1 more point.
Take turns to be the reader. Play until the pile runs out. The most points wins. In a tie, everyone wins.
Playing alone: put each card in a box, then check the back. Count your right answers out of 14.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and make the two boards. Read the three box names together. Explain that the Sun is bright, and TRAPPIST-1 is small and dim.
flow.say: A planet is too hot if its water boils away, and too cold if its water freezes. The Sun is bright, so its zone is far from it. TRAPPIST-1 is a small dim star, so its zone is very close in.
flow.kid: Make 2 boards with 3 boxes. Too hot, just right, too cold.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Goldilocks Line-Up. You set up the boards and the cards.

flow.do: Play the Earth card and the imaginary card 5 million kilometres from the Sun together. Then play the TRAPPIST-1 card for planet g. Compare.
flow.say: Earth is 150 million kilometres from the Sun. An imaginary planet is only 5 million kilometres from the Sun. Which is hotter? Planet g is about 7 million kilometres from its star, TRAPPIST-1. Is it hot or cold? Why is it different?
flow.kid: Compare 3 cards. Two planets are about the same distance from their stars, but the stars are different. Why is the answer different?

check.q: A planet is 7 million kilometres from a star. Why might it be too hot around the Sun but just right around TRAPPIST-1?
options: TRAPPIST-1 is much dimmer than the Sun
TRAPPIST-1 is bigger than the Sun
Distance does not matter
check.why: A dim star gives out far less light, so a planet can sit very close and stay cool. A bright star warms a planet at the same distance much more. Picking 'distance does not matter' misses that distance does matter, together with how bright the star is.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the same distance around two different stars.

flow.do: Play the game as the rules say. For each card, ask the player who answers to say if the world also needs air and water.
flow.say: Read the card. Put your finger on a box. Say why. Then the reader tells us the answer. Is being in the zone enough? What else does the planet need?
flow.kid: Read a card. Point to a box. Say why. Check the back.
flow.parent: The zone is only about distance. The other things that matter are a world's air, its size, and how much water it has. Mars is near the cold edge, but its thin air matters more than its distance.
flow.context: In this step, you play the game and think about what else a world needs.

flow.do: Ask what surprised them. Ask why the moons Europa and Enceladus might still have liquid water though they are in the 'too cold' box.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Europa and Enceladus are far out, in the too cold box. Why might they still have liquid water?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you? How can a far moon still have liquid water?
flow.think: If a moon is warmed from inside, does the habitable zone still matter?
flow.context: In this step, you talk about what the zone leaves out.

items.p: Which is the best description of a biosignature?
opts: A sign that living things have been there, such as a gas that would not last without them
A living creature seen through a telescope
Any gas found in a planet's air
items.why: A biosignature is a sign of life, not the life itself. It might be a gas, a chemical or a pattern that is hard to explain without life. Picking 'any gas' misses that most gases can be made without life.

items.p: Four bottles each hold warm water and sugar. Only the one with living yeast swells the balloon. Why is the bottle with sugar but no yeast important?
opts: It shows that sugar alone does not make the gas
It shows that balloons swell by themselves
It is there to use up the extra sugar
items.why: The bottle with sugar alone is the control. It stays flat, so the gas in the other bottle must come from the yeast. Picking 'balloons swell by themselves' misses that the same balloon stayed flat.

items.p: Yeast eat sugar and give out a gas called carbon ____.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the gas that swells the balloon. It is also the gas in the bubbles in idli batter and in the bread dough that rises.

items.p: Venus is hotter than Mercury because Venus is closer to the Sun.
items.why: False. Mercury is closer to the Sun. Venus is hotter because it has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat.

items.p: Sort these worlds. Around the Sun, is each one too hot, just right or too cold on its surface?
items.why: Mercury and Venus are hot, Venus because of its thick air. Earth has liquid water. Mars is cold because it is farther and has lost most of its air. Jupiter is very far from the Sun.

items.p: Match each place to what scientists have found there.
pairs: Enceladus
plumes with water, salt and hydrogen
Mars
dry lake beds and organic molecules
Titan
lakes of liquid methane
A deep-sea vent on Earth
animals that live on food made from chemicals
items.why: Each place gives a different clue about where life could live. Enceladus has an ocean, Mars once had lakes, Titan has a different liquid, and Earth's vents show life without sunlight.

items.p: Put the steps by which scientists read a faraway planet's air in order.
items: The planet crosses in front of its star
The starlight dims a tiny bit
A little starlight passes through the planet's air
Each gas takes away its own colours
Scientists read the missing colours to find the gases
items.why: The planet crosses its star, some starlight passes through the thin ring of its air, and each gas takes away its own colours. The missing colours tell scientists which gases are there.

items.p: A news story says 'Life found on a far planet'. What is the best first question to ask?
opts: What exactly was seen, and did other teams see it too?
Who is the most famous person in the story?
How many pictures does the story have?
items.why: A claim is only as good as what was observed and whether others repeat it. Fame and pictures say nothing about whether it is true.

items.p: In the Curd Zones test, cup D got its curd while the milk was too hot, and it stayed liquid. Cup A, from the fridge, set later when it was warmed. What is the difference between what cold does and what too much heat does to tiny living things?
items.a: Cold only slows them down, so they can wake up again when it warms up. Too much heat kills them for good, so they cannot wake up. So a cold world may still have sleeping life, and a world that is too hot may not.
items.why: A strong answer says that cold pauses and heat destroys, and uses it to say where life might survive.

items.p: Europa and Enceladus are far from the Sun, but may have liquid oceans. Why?
opts: Their planet's pull warms them inside, and salt keeps water liquid
They are very close to the Sun
They have a thick air like Venus
items.why: Jupiter's and Saturn's pull squeezes the moons a little more and a little less as they go round, which warms them inside. So the habitable zone is not the only place to look.

items.p: Chemosynthesis means making food from sunlight.
items.why: False. Chemosynthesis means making food from chemicals, for example from hydrogen sulfide at a deep-sea vent. Making food from sunlight is called photosynthesis.

items.p: Draw the four bottles of the Bottle Biosignature test with their balloons at the end: yeast and sugar, yeast only, sugar only, and dead yeast with sugar. Show which balloon is big and which are flat. Label the bottles that hold life.
items.a: Four bottles. The balloon on the bottle with yeast and sugar is large. The balloons on the bottle with yeast only, the bottle with sugar only and the bottle with dead yeast are flat or almost flat. Only the first is labelled as holding life.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that only the bottle with living yeast and sugar changed the air. The other three are controls.

items.p: A telescope finds a faint hint of a gas that life makes on Earth, in the air of a far planet. Three people disagree.

views.says: This is exciting. We should book more telescope time right away and look again.

views.who: Another scientist, not on the team
views.says: The hint is weak and may be noise. Other chemistry can make this gas too. Do not say life yet.
Even if the gas is real, it is only one gas. We need to see several signs that fit together.

items.ask: What would you want to see before you said that there is life on that planet? Give a reason. Then say what the person you disagree with has right.
items.a: A strong answer asks for more than one sign, observations repeated by other teams, and a check that non-living chemistry cannot explain it. It also gives the other side a fair point, for example that the hint is worth following up.
items.why: This is how real scientists treat claims. A hint is a reason to look again, not a conclusion.

items.p: A star that dims a tiny bit every few days probably has a ____ going round it.
items.why: A planet passing in front of its star blocks a little of the starlight. This is called a transit, and it is how astronomers have found thousands of planets.

items.p: Which is the strongest sign of life on a faraway planet?
opts: Several gases that fit together, seen by several teams
One gas seen once by one team
A picture of a rock that looks like a face
items.why: Strong evidence comes from several signs that fit together and are repeated by different teams. One gas seen once may be an error, and shapes in pictures can fool us.

items.p: Why is a place with liquid water but no source of energy not a good place for life?
items.a: Living things need energy to grow, move and copy themselves. Liquid water lets the chemicals of life move and meet, but without energy from light or chemicals nothing can keep going. So a place needs both water and energy.
items.why: A strong answer says that water and energy are both needed, and names where energy could come from, such as light or chemicals.

items.p: Oxygen and methane react with each other. Why are both still in Earth's air?
opts: Living things keep making both
They do not react at all
Rain brings them back
items.why: Left alone, oxygen and methane would react and fade away. They are still in our air because plants, algae and microbes keep making them. That is why the mix is a biosignature.

items.p: A hot planet's air has a lot of oxygen, but scientists think it has no life. How can that be?
opts: Strong starlight splits water and makes oxygen without life
Oxygen forms from nothing
The planet is too cold for oxygen
items.why: On some planets, strong light can split water vapour and release oxygen. So oxygen alone is a false alarm unless other signs fit with it.

items.p: Explain why finding a single gas in a planet's air is not enough to say that the planet has life.
items.a: Non-living chemistry can make many gases that life makes, for example oxygen from splitting water or methane from rocks. So a single gas may be a false alarm. Scientists want several signs that fit together, seen by several teams.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason that a gas can be made without life, and says what extra evidence would help.

items.p: A Jupiter-sized planet crossing a Sun-like star blocks about 1 part in 100 of the starlight.
items.why: True. A Jupiter-sized planet blocks about one hundredth of the light. An Earth-sized planet blocks only about one ten-thousandth, which is much harder to see.

items.p: The time between two dips in a star's light is the length of the planet's ____.
items.why: The planet goes round once between one dip and the next. That time is the planet's year.

items.p: Match each tool to what it can tell us.
pairs: A transit dip in starlight
a planet is going round the star
A spectrum with missing colours
which gases the light passed through
A radio telescope
whether any narrow signals are coming from the sky
A rover that drills rocks
which chemicals are in the rock
items.why: Each tool gives a different kind of clue. Dips find planets, spectra read air, radio telescopes listen, and rovers test rocks.

items.p: Sort these clues. Is each one a strong hint of life, not a sign, or too early to tell?
items: oxygen and methane together, being refilled
a rock shaped like a face
a weak hint of a gas, seen by only one team
a balloon swelling on a bottle of yeast and sugar
a round pit in a Moon rock
items.why: Gases being refilled and gas from a bottle of yeast point to something making them. A rock shape or a crater can be made without life. A weak hint seen once needs more checking.

items.p: Put the steps of a Drake chain in order, from the largest number to the smallest.
items: Stars with a planet in the habitable zone
Civilisations sending signals we can hear
items.why: Each step keeps only a share of the step before, so the numbers get smaller down the chain.

items.p: In a Drake chain, which change would make the answer drop the most?
opts: Dividing by 1,000,000 instead of 10 at the step where life becomes able to build machines
Dividing the stars by 5 instead of by 2
Adding one more star
items.why: Dividing by a million is a far bigger cut than dividing by 10. This is why the answer depends on the steps we know least about.

items.p: In the Curd Zones test, the cup of milk and curd in the fridge did not set, but it set later when it was moved to a warm box. What does this say about cold, and why could it matter for a very cold icy moon?
items.a: Cold does not kill tiny living things. It pauses them, and they wake up when warmed. So microbes could sleep in the cold, and life could survive in a cold place for a long time. It matters because an icy moon may keep sleeping life, or its inside may be warm enough for life to be awake.
items.why: A strong answer says that cold pauses life and does not end it, and links this to icy places.

items.p: Titan's lakes are made of liquid water.
items.why: False. Titan's lakes are made of liquid methane and ethane. It is too cold there, about minus 179 degrees, for water to be liquid.

items.p: A planet 7 million kilometres from a dim red dwarf may be just right, but a planet 7 million kilometres from the Sun would be far too hot. Why?
opts: The red dwarf gives out much less light than the Sun
The red dwarf is much bigger than the Sun
Distance never matters
items.why: The habitable zone depends on how bright the star is. A dim star gives out little light, so its zone is very close in.

items.p: Draw a star with a planet crossing in front of it. Below it, draw a graph of the star's brightness over time. Mark the dip, and mark the length of the planet's year.
items.a: A star with a small planet in front of it. Below, a flat line with a small dip, and a second dip later. An arrow between the two dips labelled the planet's year.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the dip happens when the planet is in front, and that the time between dips is the length of the year.

items.p: A space agency has money for one new mission. Two scientists want different worlds, and a taxpayer asks a question.

views.says: Rovers are already working on Mars and samples are waiting. A new mission to bring them back would cost less and give clear results.
Enceladus sprays its ocean into space. A spacecraft can sample it without landing, and it has chemicals life could use.
Why spend so much on life in space when there are problems with water and air on Earth?

items.ask: Which view do you find the most convincing, and why? Say what the other views get right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and gives reasons that use water, energy and ease of testing. It also gives the others a fair point, for example that learning how life works in space can also help us look after life on Earth.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Good answers use the science of where life could live and treat the other views fairly.

items.p: Making food from chemicals, not from sunlight, is called chemo____.
items.why: Chemosynthesis lets bacteria at deep-sea vents make food from chemicals. It is why life can live in places that sunlight never reaches.

items.p: Bacteria at a deep-sea vent make food from hydrogen sulfide and oxygen. Why does that matter for the dark ocean of Europa?
opts: It shows that life can live in the dark if there are chemicals to react
It shows that Europa has deep-sea vents
It shows that sunlight reaches Europa's ocean
items.why: Life does not need sunlight if it has another source of energy. Whether Europa has such a source is not yet known. Picking 'shows that Europa has vents' is a guess that is not yet proved.

items.p: Look at the chart of balloon sizes at 40 minutes. Which two bottles together show that the gas comes from living yeast, and not just from the yeast powder?
opts: A, with living yeast, and D, with boiled yeast
B, with yeast only, and C, with sugar only
C, with sugar only, and D, with boiled yeast
items.why: Bottles A and D have the same powder and the same sugar. The only difference is that the yeast in D was killed. A swelled and D did not, so living yeast made the gas.

chart.title: Made-up example: size round the balloon at 40 minutes

items.p: In a yeast test, the bottle with yeast but no added sugar swelled the balloon by 2 centimetres. Give one reason why it was not completely flat, other than a measuring mistake.
items.a: Yeast powder can hold a little sugar, or the water may have held a little. The yeast ate this small amount and made a small amount of gas. A balloon fitted loosely might also have settled slightly.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason that is about the experiment and says that a small result is different from a large one.

items.p: Star P dips by 1 part in 1,000 every 4 days. Star Q dips by 1 part in 100 every 6 days. Which statement is correct?
opts: Q's planet is bigger, and P's planet has the shorter year
P's planet is bigger, and Q's planet has the shorter year
Both planets are the same size
items.why: A deeper dip means a bigger planet, so Q's planet is bigger. A 4-day year is shorter than a 6-day year, so P's planet goes round faster and is closer to its star.

items.p: A planet with a 4-day year and a planet with a 6-day year go round the same kind of star. The planet with the shorter year is ____ to its star.
items.why: A planet closer to its star goes round faster, so its year is shorter.

items.p: A Drake chain starts with 100 billion stars. Divide by 5, then by 10, then by 1,000, then by 100. How many are left? Show each step.
items.a: 100,000,000,000 divided by 5 is 20,000,000,000. Divided by 10 is 2,000,000,000. Divided by 1,000 is 2,000,000. Divided by 100 is 20,000. So 20,000 are left.
items.why: A strong answer shows each division, with the right number of zeros. You can check by multiplying back.

items.p: Two Drake chains use the same stars. One divides by 1,000 at the step where life starts, and the other divides by 2. By how many times do their answers differ?
opts: 500 times
2 times
1,000 times
items.why: Dividing by 1,000 gives an answer 500 times smaller than dividing by 2, because 1,000 divided by 2 is 500. A single guess can change the whole answer by a huge factor.

items.p: A radio signal heard once and never again is strong proof of an alien civilisation.
items.why: False. Science needs a signal that can be checked again by others. The 1977 Wow! signal was never heard again, so nobody could test what made it.

items.p: Match each claim to the test that would help the most.
pairs: Spots on a Mars rock came from past life
study the sample in laboratories on Earth
A hint of a gas on a far planet means life
more observations by other teams
Mars's methane is made by microbes
measure methane in many places and seasons
A strange signal came from space
listen again with a second telescope
items.why: Each claim needs a test that can show it wrong. Samples, repeats and checks by others are how scientists decide.

items.p: Is a virus alive? Three people disagree.

views.says: Yes. Viruses carry a code, copy the code and change over many generations.
Not on their own. Viruses cannot make more viruses without a host cell, and they use no energy by themselves.
It depends on your definition. A virus is on the edge, and that tells us our definitions are too simple.

items.ask: Which view do you find the most convincing, and why? Say what the other views get right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and says which signs of life it counts, such as energy use, a code or growth. It gives the others a fair point, for example that the answer depends on the definition.
items.why: This is an open question. A virus shows some signs of life and not others, which is exactly the problem for scientists who look for life elsewhere.

items.p: Suppose microbes found on Mars used the same DNA code as life on Earth. Give two possible reasons.
items.a: Life on Earth and Mars may have a common origin, if rocks knocked off one planet carried microbes to the other. Or the microbes may be from Earth, carried there by mistake on a spacecraft. Either way, scientists would need more checks.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons and says that it matters to check for contamination.

items.p: Why does a spacecraft that flies through a plume have to collect everything in one pass?
opts: It moves so fast that it has no second chance
The plume is very cold
The spacecraft is too heavy to turn
items.why: A spacecraft flies through a plume at a very high speed, in a few seconds. Its instruments must work during that pass.

items.p: Put these in order from the weakest evidence of life to the strongest.
items: A hill that looks like a face in a photo
One weak hint of a gas seen by one team
Several gases that fit together, seen by several teams
A living sample growing in a laboratory
items.why: A shape can fool us easily. A single weak hint is better, but could be noise. Several signs seen by many teams are stronger. A sample growing and copying itself in a lab is the best proof.

items.p: Draw the habitable zone around a bright star and around a dim red star. Put a planet in the zone of each.
items.a: Two stars. The bright star has a ring that is far out, with a planet in it. The dim red star has a ring that is very close in, with a planet in it. A note says the dim star's zone is much closer.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the zone moves with the star's brightness, so a dim star has a zone close in.

items.p: A headline says 'Alien life found'. The scientists saw a faint hint of a gas that life makes on Earth, in the air of a far planet, and other teams do not agree. Write a fairer headline.
items.a: For example: Telescope sees a faint hint of a gas that life makes on Earth, but other teams disagree. A fair headline says what was seen, how sure the scientists are, and that others do not agree.
items.why: A strong answer says only what was observed and gives the level of doubt.

items.p: A world outside the habitable zone cannot have liquid water.
items.why: False. Europa and Enceladus are far outside the Sun's zone and probably have oceans under their ice, kept liquid by heat from inside.

items.p: Which is the best reason to bring a Mars rock sample back to laboratories on Earth?
opts: Big instruments and many teams can check it in ways a rover cannot
The rock will be warmer on Earth
Rocks are lighter on Earth
items.why: Laboratories on Earth have larger and more exact instruments than a rover can carry, and many teams can check the same sample. This is how a claim can be tested.

experiments.title: Bottle Biosignature: which bottles hold life?
experiments.context: This is a test of how living things change the air around them. You set up four sealed bottles with balloons on top. You never open them or look at the yeast. You tell which bottles hold living yeast by the balloons alone, the way a scientist reads the air of a far planet.
experiments.question: Which bottle will blow up its balloon: yeast and sugar, yeast with no sugar, sugar with no yeast, or sugar with yeast that has been killed by boiling?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which bottle will swell its balloon the most? Which will not swell at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every bottle gets the same amount of warm water, the same kind of balloon, and the same warm place. Only what is in the bottle changes. You measure all four balloons at the same times. Bottle C, with no yeast, and bottle D, with dead yeast, are the controls. They show what the sugar does without living yeast.
