materials.item: 4 clean plastic bottles of the same size, 500 millilitres, labelled A, B, C and D
4 balloons of the same kind, new, not blown up before
1 packet of dry baking yeast, about 7 grams
sugar, 3 tablespoons, and a teaspoon and a tablespoon for measuring
warm water from the tap or a kettle, cooled until it feels like a comfortable bath, about 40 degrees, never hot
a big bowl or bucket of the same warm water, deep enough to stand the bottles in
a small pan, a stove and a cup, for a grown-up to boil and cool some yeast
a piece of string 50 centimetres long and a ruler, to measure round the balloons
a marker, a timer and a tray

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the boiling. Water for the bottles should feel like a comfortable bath, never hot. Do not eat the yeast, and keep the yeast powder out of eyes. Balloons are a choking risk for children under eight, so keep them away from small children, and nobody should blow them up by mouth or put them in their mouths. Wash hands afterwards.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw each bottle at 40 minutes, with its balloon. Draw a bar chart of the balloon sizes at 40 minutes.

setup.art: Four bottles in a row labelled A to D, with yeast, sugar and warm water being added in different amounts, shown by small labels.
setup.caption: 1. Set up four bottles: A yeast and sugar, B yeast only, C sugar only, D dead yeast and sugar.

setup.art: A child fitting a balloon over the neck of each bottle, and the four bottles standing in a bowl of warm water.
setup.caption: 2. Fit a balloon on each bottle. Stand the bottles in the warm water.

setup.art: A child wrapping a string around the fattest part of a swollen balloon and then laying the string against a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Every 10 minutes, wrap a string around each balloon. Measure the string.

setup.art: Four bottles at the end of the test, only the first with a large swollen balloon, the others flat.
setup.caption: 4. Look at the four balloons. Which bottle holds life?

flow.do: Show your child the four bottles, the yeast, the sugar and the balloons. Say what will go into each bottle. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We have four bottles. A gets yeast and sugar. B gets yeast and no sugar. C gets sugar and no yeast. D gets sugar and yeast that has been boiled. Which balloon will swell the most? Which will not swell at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four bottles with different things in them. Which balloon swells the most? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a balloon might swell on one bottle and not the others?
good: Something in the bottle makes a gas.
The yeast is alive and eats the sugar.
The sugar makes gas when it gets warm.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not tell your child yet what yeast does.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle Biosignature test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up boils 100 millilitres of water in the pan, adds 1 teaspoon of yeast, and boils the mixture for 2 minutes. Cool the mixture until it is warm. Meanwhile, pour 150 millilitres of warm water into each of the four bottles.
flow.say: Yeast is a living thing, so we are going to kill some of it by boiling. That will be the yeast in bottle D. While it cools, we put warm water in all four bottles.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to boil some yeast. Pour warm water into all 4 bottles.
flow.parent: The boiled yeast must be cooled to warm, not hot, before it goes in the bottle. The water in the bottles should feel like a comfortable bath. Water that is too hot kills the yeast, and water that is too cold slows the yeast a lot.

check.q: Why do we use boiled yeast in bottle D?
options: To check that the gas comes from living yeast, not from yeast powder
To make the water hotter
To save time
check.why: Boiling kills yeast but leaves the same powder. If bottle D stays flat while bottle A swells, the gas comes from living yeast, not just from the powder. Picking 'hotter' misses that the boiled yeast is cooled first.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up boils some yeast so that the yeast die, and you pour warm water into all four bottles.

flow.do: Add the contents to the bottles. A gets 1 teaspoon of yeast and 1 tablespoon of sugar. B gets 1 teaspoon of yeast. C gets 1 tablespoon of sugar. D gets the boiled yeast and 1 tablespoon of sugar. Swirl each for 30 seconds. Fit a balloon on each and stand them in the warm water bath. Note the time.
flow.say: A gets yeast and sugar. B gets yeast only. C gets sugar only. D gets dead yeast and sugar. Swirl each bottle for thirty seconds, fit the balloon on, and stand it in the bath. Now we start the timer.
flow.kid: Add the yeast and sugar to each bottle as the labels say. Swirl. Fit the balloons.
flow.parent: Use the same teaspoon and tablespoon for each bottle, level, not heaped. Check that each balloon fits on tightly, or gas will leak out. Top up the warm bath with warm water after 15 minutes, if it has cooled.
flow.context: In this step, you put the yeast and sugar in the bottles, fit the balloons and start the timer.

flow.do: At 10 minutes, wrap the string round the widest part of each balloon, one at a time. Hold the string against the ruler. Write the length. At 20 minutes, do the same. If a balloon is flat, write 0.
flow.say: Ten minutes have passed. Wrap the string around the fattest part of the balloon. Now put the string on the ruler. How long is it? Do the same for each bottle. We do it again at twenty minutes.
flow.kid: At 10 and 20 minutes, wrap string round each balloon. Measure the string.
flow.parent: The bottles need not be opened at any time. Do not shake them. A balloon that is only a little swollen may look flat, so lift it gently and look from the side.

check.q: By 20 minutes, only balloon A has started to swell. What does that suggest?
options: Yeast and sugar together are making a gas
Sugar alone makes gas when warm
Balloon A is a different kind
check.why: Balloon C, with sugar alone, stayed flat. Balloon B, with yeast alone, stayed flat too. Only bottle A, with both, swelled. So it is the yeast using the sugar that makes the gas. Picking 'a different kind of balloon' misses that all four balloons were the same.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the four balloons at 10 and 20 minutes.

flow.do: At 30 minutes and 40 minutes, measure the balloons again in the same way. Write the lengths. Smell each bottle by sniffing at the neck of the bottle, but do not open it.
flow.say: At thirty minutes, measure the balloons again. At forty minutes, measure once more. Can you smell anything near the neck of the bottle? What does bottle A smell like? Does it smell like anything you have at home?
flow.kid: Measure at 30 and 40 minutes. Sniff near the neck of each bottle.
flow.parent: Expected: balloon A swells steadily, the others stay flat or nearly flat. Bottle A smells like bread or batter. If balloon A has not swelled after 30 minutes, the yeast may be old or the water too hot or cold. Write it down, and try again with fresh yeast and bath-warm water.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the balloons at 30 and 40 minutes and smell the bottles.

flow.do: Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw that shows it, and why they think it happened. Then ask your child to be a space probe that can see only the balloons. Draw a bar chart of the balloon sizes at 40 minutes.
flow.say: Let's put it together. First, what do you think now? Second, what did you see that shows it? Third, why do you think it happened? Now pretend you are a space probe that can see only the balloons. Which bottles would you say hold life?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened. Then pretend you can see only the balloons.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: living yeast change the gas in the bottle. What I saw: only the bottle with yeast and sugar swelled the balloon. The dead yeast and the sugar alone did nothing. Why: living yeast eat sugar and give out carbon dioxide gas, and the gas swells the balloon. A probe that saw only the balloons would say bottle A holds life, and it would be right. But a probe seeing only a swollen balloon could be fooled by something else that makes gas, so a scientist would want a second sign. Give this last part only after your child has given their own ideas.
flow.think: What other thing could swell a balloon on a bottle, without any life?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the balloons show, and you play the part of a probe that sees only the gas.

experiments.title: Curd Zones: how warm must it be for curd bacteria to live?
experiments.context: This is a test of how warmth decides where tiny living things can live, like a habitable zone for curd bacteria. You put the same milk and the same spoon of curd in four places, one very cold, one cool, one warm and one too hot. Then you see where the milk sets into curd overnight.
experiments.question: In which place will milk set into curd overnight: a fridge, a kitchen counter, a warm box, or a cup that was too hot at the start?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which cup will set first? Which will never set? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every cup gets the same amount of the same milk and 1 teaspoon of the same curd. Only the place, and so the warmth, changes. Cup D is the only one that starts too hot, because the curd goes into milk that has just been boiled. You look at all four at the same time next morning.
results_table: Did it set by morning? (yes, a little or no)
What happened when I moved it to the warm box

materials.item: 4 small steel katoris or cups with lids or small plates, labelled A, B, C and D
1 litre of milk, boiled by a grown-up
4 teaspoons of fresh curd as a starter, from a pot of curd that is mildly sour and has not been heated
a small insulated box or tiffin box, with a bottle of warm water inside, as the warm place
a fridge shelf and a space on the kitchen counter
a thermometer, if you have one, a spoon and a marker

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the milk and pours the hot milk. Hot milk burns, so keep children back. Keep all cups covered and clean. Do not eat what is in cups A and D. If any cup looks pink, fizzy or smells rotten, throw it away. Wash hands.

schedule.what: Guess. A grown-up boils the milk. Put curd in the four cups and put each in its place.
Next morning, look at the four cups. Move cups A and D to the warm box. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw each cup and show whether the curd set or stayed liquid.

setup.art: Four labelled steel katoris in a row, each holding a spoonful of white curd.
setup.caption: 1. Label four cups. Put one teaspoon of curd in each.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm milk into three cups and hot steaming milk into the fourth.
setup.caption: 2. Pour in the milk. Cup D gets milk that has just boiled.

setup.art: Four cups in four places: a fridge, a kitchen counter, a small insulated box with a warm bottle and a counter beside the stove.
setup.caption: 3. Put each cup in its place, with the lid on.

setup.art: In the morning, one cup of firm set curd tilted without spilling, and three cups of liquid milk.
setup.caption: 4. Next morning, tilt each cup gently. Which has set?

flow.do: Show your child the four cups, the milk and the curd. Say where each cup will go. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will put the same milk and the same curd in four places. A goes in the fridge. B stays on the kitchen counter. C goes in a warm box. D gets milk that was just boiled. Which cup will set first? Which will never set? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four cups in four places. Which one makes curd? Which does not? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think one place might make curd and another not?
good: The curd bacteria like warmth.
Cold makes them stop.
Hot milk would kill them.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not say yet that curd is made by bacteria.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Curd Zones test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up boils the milk. Pour a little hot milk into cup D straight away, and stir in 1 teaspoon of curd while it is steaming. Let the rest cool until you can keep a clean finger in it for 10 seconds, about 40 to 45 degrees. Pour 100 millilitres of the cooled milk into cups A, B and C.
flow.say: Cup D gets the curd while the milk is still steaming hot. For the others, we wait until the milk is warm like a bath. Keep a clean finger in it for ten seconds. If it hurts, it is too hot.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils the milk. Wait until it is warm. Pour it into cups A, B and C.
flow.parent: Do the finger test with a clean finger. If you have a thermometer, the milk for A, B and C should be 40 to 45 degrees. Curd bacteria die quickly above about 60 degrees, so the bacteria in cup D will die at once.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up boils the milk and pours it into the cups. Cup D gets the curd while the milk is too hot.

flow.do: Stir 1 teaspoon of curd into each of cups A, B and C. Cover all four cups. Put A in the fridge. Put B on the kitchen counter. Put C in the insulated box with a bottle of warm water. Put D on the counter.
flow.say: A goes in the fridge. B stays out in the kitchen. C goes in the warm box. D is the one that was too hot. Now we wait all night.
flow.kid: Stir a spoon of curd into cups A, B and C. Cover every cup. Put A in the fridge, B and D on the counter, and C in the warm box.

check.q: Why do we put the same spoon of the same curd in every cup?
options: So only the warmth changes
So all the cups taste the same
So we can eat all of them
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one cup got more curd, you would not know if the warmth or the curd made it set faster.

flow.context: In this step, you stir curd into the cups and put each cup in its place.

flow.do: Next morning, look at each cup. Tilt it gently. Write whether the milk has set into curd or is still liquid. Smell each cup. Do not taste cups A and D.
flow.say: Good morning, curd cups. Tilt each one gently. Has it set, or does it still flow like milk? Smell it. Is it sour? Write down what you find.
flow.kid: Tilt each cup. Is it curd or milk? Smell it. Write what you find.
flow.wait: Look at the cups next morning
flow.parent: Expected: cup C, in the warm box, has set. Cup B has probably set in warm weather, but may be softer or still liquid on a cold night. Cup A is still liquid. Cup D is still liquid, because the curd bacteria were killed. If your result is different, write it down. It is still a result.

check.q: Cup D stayed liquid. What is the best explanation?
options: The milk was so hot that it killed the curd bacteria
The curd was old
The cup was too small
check.why: Curd bacteria die in milk that is too hot. Cup D had the same curd as the others. Picking 'the curd was old' misses that the same curd made the other cups work.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the four cups the next morning.

flow.do: Move cups A and D into the warm box with a fresh bottle of warm water. Leave them for a few hours and check again. Then ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Now we move the fridge cup and the too-hot cup into the warm box. Which one do you think will set later? Why? Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Move cups A and D into the warm box. Then say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.wait: Check cups A and D again later the same day
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: curd bacteria need a warm place, cold puts them to sleep and too much heat kills them. What I saw: C set, A and D stayed liquid. Why: warmth makes the bacteria grow and sour the milk, and then the milk sets. Cold only slows them, and cup A usually sets later when warmed. Cup D never sets, because heat killed the bacteria. This is like Earth's cold places, where microbes can sleep, and its boiling places, where most cannot live.
flow.think: A planet that is too cold might still have sleeping life, and a planet that is too hot might not. What does that say about where to look?
flow.context: In this step, you move the two cups that did not set into the warm box and think about what the test showed.

activities.title: Earth From Far Away: how would a visitor know we are alive?
activities.context: This is a thinking activity to start the unit. You imagine a visitor looking at Earth through a telescope from very far away. You list the signs of life they could see, and work out which signs are hardest to fake.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a globe or a picture of Earth, if you have one

schedule.what: Imagine a visitor far from Earth. List five signs of life they could see. Rank them from easiest to hardest to fake.

activities.record: A list of five signs of life on Earth that a far-off visitor might see, ranked from the easiest to the hardest to fake.

setup.art: A visitor in a spacecraft looking through a telescope at a small blue-and-white Earth in the distance.
setup.caption: 1. A visitor looks at Earth from very far away.

setup.art: A page with five boxes on it, each with a small drawing: green patches, night lights, oxygen, radio waves and clouds.
setup.caption: 2. List five signs of life a visitor could see.

flow.do: Ask your child to imagine a visitor far away looking at Earth, without being able to come closer. Ask them to list five signs of life the visitor might see or detect.
flow.say: A visitor is far from Earth and cannot land. She has a telescope. What signs of life on Earth could she see or detect from there? Think of colours, lights, gases and signals.
flow.kid: A visitor looks at Earth from far away. List 5 signs of life she could see.

ask.q: What on Earth could show life from very far away?
good: Green patches of forest, which change with the seasons.
Oxygen in the air.
Lights of cities at night, and radio signals.

flow.parent: Possible answers: green land that changes colour with the seasons, oxygen and methane in the air, lights of cities at night, radio signals from phones and towers, cloud patterns. Accept any sensible sign.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Earth From Far Away activity. You list signs of life a far-off visitor could see.

flow.do: Ask your child to rank the five signs from the easiest to fake with no life to the hardest to fake. Talk about which sign would still be there if all the people on Earth vanished.
flow.say: Now rank the signs. Which one could non-living things fake easily? Which one would be hardest to fake? And which sign would still be there if all the people vanished?
flow.kid: Rank your 5 signs. Which is easiest to fake? Which is hardest?

check.q: If all the people on Earth vanished, which sign of life would a far-off visitor still see?
options: Oxygen and methane in the air, kept there by plants and microbes
The lights of cities at night
Radio signals from towers
check.why: Plants, algae and microbes keep making oxygen and methane, whether or not people are there. City lights and radio signals would fade as the machines stopped. The gases made by plants and microbes are the oldest sign of life on Earth.

flow.think: Which of these signs would be best for finding microbes, not people?
flow.context: In this step, you rank the signs from the easiest to fake to the hardest to fake.

activities.title: Planet Hunter's Graph: find two planets from dips in starlight
activities.context: This is a data activity. You get the brightness of two stars, measured every day. You draw a graph of each, find the dips made by a planet crossing the star, and work out how long each planet's year is and which one is bigger.

materials.item: graph paper or squared paper
a ruler and a pencil
coloured pencils, two colours

schedule.what: Draw a graph for each star. Find the dips. Work out the length of each planet's year and which planet is bigger.

activities.record: Two graphs, one for each star, with the dips marked. The length of each planet's year in days. Which planet is bigger, and why you think so.

setup.art: A sheet of graph paper with days from 1 to 18 along the bottom and brightness from 985 to 1000 up the side, and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the axes: days along the bottom, brightness up the side.

setup.art: Dots plotted on the graph joined by a line, with three clear dips marked with arrows.
setup.caption: 2. Plot the dots for Star X. Join them. Mark the dips.

setup.art: A second graph in a different colour for Star Y, with four tiny dips.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same for Star Y. Compare the dips.

flow.do: Explain that a star dims a tiny bit when a planet passes in front. Read out the data for Star X. The brightness is 1000 on every day from 1 to 18. It is 990 on days 5, 11 and 17. Ask your child to guess how the graph will look.
flow.say: A planet is too faint to see, but when it crosses in front of its star, the star dims a tiny bit. Star X has a brightness of 1000 on most days, but 990 on days 5, 11 and 17. What will the graph look like? What does a dip mean?
flow.kid: A planet crossing a star makes it dim. Star X has a brightness of 1000, except on days 5, 11 and 17, when it is 990.

ask.q: What do you think the dips tell us about the planet?
good: There is a planet crossing in front of the star.
The time between the dips is the planet's year.
A bigger dip means a bigger planet.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The data are made up, but real transits look like this. A brightness of 1000 stands for the star's normal light, so 990 means 10 parts in 1,000 less.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Planet Hunter's Graph. You read the data and guess what the graph will show.

flow.do: Draw the graph for Star X. Put days 1 to 18 along the bottom and brightness 985 to 1000 up the side. Plot a dot for each day. Join the dots with a line. Mark each dip with an arrow.
flow.say: Days go along the bottom, from 1 to 18. Brightness goes up the side, from 985 to 1000. Put a dot for each day. Most dots are at the top. Three dots are lower. Join them up. What do you see?
flow.kid: Draw a graph. Days along the bottom. Brightness up the side. Plot Star X.

check.q: Star X dips on days 5, 11 and 17. How long is the planet's year?
options: 6 days, the time from one dip to the next
5 days, the first dip
17 days, the last dip
check.why: The planet goes round once between each dip. From day 5 to day 11 is 6 days, and from day 11 to day 17 is 6 days. Picking '5' or '17' confuses the day of a dip with the time between dips.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the graph for Star X and find the length of its planet's year.

flow.do: Now draw Star Y on the same graph in a different colour. Star Y is 1000 on every day from 1 to 18, except 999 on days 3, 7, 11, 15. Find the length of its planet's year.
flow.say: Now Star Y. It is 1000 every day, except 999 on days 3, 7, 11 and 15. Plot it in another colour on the same graph. How long is its planet's year? Which dip is deeper?
flow.kid: Draw Star Y in another colour. Dips on days 3, 7, 11, 15. How long is its year?
flow.parent: Star Y's planet has a 4-day year. Its dips are tiny, only 1 part in 1,000. Star X's dips are 10 parts in 1,000, which is 1 part in 100, the size of a Jupiter-sized planet in front of a Sun-like star.
flow.context: In this step, you draw Star Y and find its planet's year.

flow.do: Compare the two planets. Ask which is bigger and which is closer to its star. Then ask your child three things: what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which planet blocks more light, X or Y? So which is bigger? Which has the shorter year? A planet with a shorter year is closer to its star. What do you think? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Which planet is bigger? Which is closer to its star? Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: planet X is bigger and planet Y is closer to its star. What I saw: X made a deeper dip, and Y's dips came every 4 days. Why: a bigger planet blocks more light, and a planet closer to its star goes round faster. An Earth-sized planet would block only about 1 part in 10,000, so it would be very hard to see.
flow.think: How would you check that the dips are a planet and not something else, like a star spot?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the two planets and say what the graphs show.

activities.title: A Drake Chain: how many neighbours might there be?
activities.context: This is an estimating activity. You follow a chain of guesses, step by step, from the number of stars in our galaxy to the number of civilisations who might send signals. You try three sets of guesses, and see how much the answer depends on them.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a calculator, if you have one

schedule.what: Start with 100 billion stars. Try three sets of guesses. Compare the answers.

activities.record: Three chains of numbers, one for each set of guesses, ending in a number of civilisations.

setup.art: A funnel with 100,000,000,000 stars written at the top and four boxes underneath, each with a one in N share.
setup.caption: 1. Start with 100 billion stars at the top of the funnel.

setup.art: A child dividing 100,000,000,000 by 5, then writing the answer below it on a piece of paper.
setup.caption: 2. Divide by each guess in turn. Write down each answer.

setup.art: Three funnels side by side, one with a large number at the bottom, one with a medium number and one with a very small number.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the three answers.

flow.do: Write down 100,000,000,000 stars. Explain the four steps. First, stars with a planet in the habitable zone. Second, planets where life starts. Third, places where life becomes able to build machines. Fourth, civilisations who send signals while we listen. Ask for a guess about the final number.
flow.say: Our galaxy has at least 100 billion stars. At each step, only a share of them go on to the next. Which steps do you think are easy, and which are hard? Guess how many civilisations will be left at the end.
flow.kid: 100 billion stars. 4 steps, each keeps only some. Guess how many are left at the end.

ask.q: Which step do you think is the hardest, and why?
good: Life starting, because we only know of one place.
Becoming able to build machines, which took billions of years on Earth.
Sending signals at the right time, so we can hear.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Drake Chain activity. You set up the chain and guess.

flow.do: Do the optimist chain. Step 1: divide 100,000,000,000 by 5. Step 2: divide the answer by 2. Step 3: divide the answer by 10. Step 4: divide the answer by 10. Write each answer.
flow.say: The optimist says one star in five has a planet in the zone. One such planet in two gets life. One in ten becomes able to build machines. One in ten sends signals we can hear. Divide step by step. What is left?
flow.kid: Divide 100 billion by 5. Then by 2. Then by 10. Then by 10. What is left?
flow.parent: The answers are 20,000,000,000, then 10,000,000,000, then 1,000,000,000, then 100,000,000. The optimist ends with 100 million civilisations.

check.q: In the optimist chain, how many civilisations are left at the end?
options: 100 million
100 thousand
check.why: 100,000,000,000 divided by 5 is 20,000,000,000. Divided by 2 is 10,000,000,000. Divided by 10 is 1,000,000,000. Divided by 10 again is 100,000,000, which is 100 million. Check each step by multiplying back.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the optimist chain.

flow.do: Do the cautious chain. Step 1: divide 100,000,000,000 by 5. Step 2: divide by 10. Step 3: divide by 1,000. Step 4: divide by 100. Write each answer. Then try a very cautious chain with step 2 divided by 1,000 and step 3 divided by 1,000,000.
flow.say: The cautious person says life starts in one place in ten. One in a thousand becomes able to build machines. One in a hundred sends signals we can hear. What is left? Then a very cautious person says life starts in one place in a thousand, and only one in a million of those becomes able to build machines. What is left now?
flow.kid: Cautious: divide by 5, 10, 1,000 and 100. What is left? Then try a very cautious chain.
flow.parent: The cautious chain gives 20,000,000,000 then 2,000,000,000 then 2,000,000 then 20,000. The very cautious chain gives 20,000,000,000 then 20,000,000 then 20, then 0.2 at the last step. That is less than one, so it means we may be alone in our galaxy. The same starting number gives answers from 100 million to less than one.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the cautious chain and a very cautious chain.

flow.do: Compare the three answers. Ask which step changed the answer the most. Then ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Look at the three answers. They are very different. Which step made the biggest difference? What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Compare the 3 answers. Which step changed the answer most? Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: the answer depends mostly on the guesses we know least about. What I saw: the answer ran from 100 million to less than one. Why: the steps about life starting and becoming intelligent are the least known, and each one divides the answer by a very big number. This does not tell us the answer. It tells us which things we most need to find out.
flow.think: Which number would you most like to know, to make the answer better?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the three chains and say what they show.

activities.title: Colours Taken Away: how light shows what is in the air
activities.context: This is a model of how scientists read a planet's air from the light that passes through it. A coloured sheet takes away some colours from a rainbow, as a gas takes away its own colours from starlight.

materials.item: an old CD or DVD, shiny side
a torch or phone torch
sheets of coloured cellophane: red, green and yellow
a darkened room and a white wall or sheet of paper

activities.safety: Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Keep the beam pointing at the CD and the wall.

schedule.what: Make a rainbow with a CD and a torch. Put coloured cellophane in the beam. See which colours go missing.

activities.record: Draw the rainbow with no cellophane. Draw it again with each coloured sheet, showing which colours are missing.

setup.art: A torch beam shining on a tilted CD in a dark room, with a rainbow band on the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Shine the torch on the CD. Tilt it until a rainbow shows on the wall.

setup.art: A red cellophane sheet held in front of the torch, and the rainbow on the wall showing only a red band.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a coloured sheet in front of the torch. Which colours go missing?

setup.art: Three small rainbow strips side by side, each with a different part missing.
setup.caption: 3. Try each coloured sheet. Draw what is missing.

flow.do: Explain that a gas takes away its own colours from the light. Show the CD and the cellophane. Ask your child to guess what a red sheet in front of the torch will do to the rainbow.
flow.say: Starlight is a rainbow of colours. When it passes through a planet's air, each gas takes away its own colours. Today, a coloured sheet is our gas. What will a red sheet do to the rainbow? Which colours will disappear? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A coloured sheet takes away some colours. What will red do to a rainbow? Why?

ask.q: Which colours do you think a red sheet will take away?
good: Everything except red.
Blue and green.
I do not know.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Colours Taken Away activity. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Darken the room. Hold the CD by its edges, shiny side towards the torch. Shine the torch at the CD from 30 centimetres. Tilt the CD until a rainbow band shows on the wall or on white paper.
flow.say: Hold the CD by its edges. Shine the torch onto the shiny side. Tilt it a little. Do you see a rainbow on the wall? Which colour is at the top? Which at the bottom?
flow.kid: Hold the CD by the edges. Shine the torch on it. Tilt it to find a rainbow.
flow.parent: It may take a minute to find the angle. Keep the room as dark as you can, and make the torch beam small by holding it close to the CD. If you have no CD, a glass of water in strong sunshine on a windowsill can also throw a rainbow on the wall.
flow.context: In this step, you make a rainbow on the wall with a CD and a torch.

flow.do: Hold the red sheet in front of the torch. Look at the rainbow. Write which colours are missing. Do the same with the green sheet and the yellow sheet.
flow.say: Hold the red sheet in front of the torch. What happens to the rainbow? Which colours are gone? Now try green, and then yellow. Write down what is missing each time.
flow.kid: Hold a coloured sheet in front of the torch. Which rainbow colours go missing?

check.q: A red sheet in front of the torch leaves only red in the rainbow. What does this show?
options: The sheet takes away the other colours from the light
The sheet makes red light
The sheet is hot
check.why: The torch gives out all colours. The red sheet lets red through and takes away the rest, so only red is left on the wall. Picking 'makes red light' misses that the light came from the torch.

flow.parent: Expected: red leaves only the red end. Green leaves mostly the green part. Yellow takes away the blue and violet end, leaving red, orange, yellow and green. Real gases are more precise. Each takes away very narrow lines of colour, like a barcode.
flow.context: In this step, you put coloured sheets in front of the torch and see which colours go missing.

flow.do: Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Connect the coloured sheets to a planet's air. Ask how missing colours could tell us a gas is there.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Now, if starlight passed through a planet's air and some colours were missing, what could scientists work out?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened. How could missing colours show a gas?
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: a coloured thing takes away some colours from white light. What I saw: with the red sheet only red was left. Why: the sheet lets some colours through and stops the others. A gas does the same, with its own set of missing colours. By seeing which colours are missing, scientists can tell which gases the light passed through.
flow.context: In this step, you connect your test to the way scientists read the air of faraway planets.

activities.title: Alive or Not? Argue it out
activities.context: This is a talking activity. You take eight things and decide which are alive, using a list of signs of life. Some are easy, and some are not. This is the problem scientists face when they look for life elsewhere.

materials.item: paper and a pencil, to draw a table
8 small cards or slips of paper

schedule.what: Write eight things on cards. For each, tick the signs of life it shows. Decide, and argue about the hard ones.

activities.record: A table with eight things down the side and six signs of life across the top, with ticks. Your decision on each.

setup.art: Eight cards laid out in a row: a flame, a dry seed, yeast, a virus, a robot vacuum cleaner, a growing crystal, a banyan tree and a mule.
setup.caption: 1. Write eight things on cards.

setup.art: A table with the eight things down the side and six signs across the top: uses energy, grows, responds, copies itself, changes over generations, made of cells.
setup.caption: 2. Tick the signs each thing shows.

flow.do: Write these eight things on cards: a candle flame, a dry seed, yeast in sugar water, a virus, a robot vacuum cleaner, a growing salt crystal, a banyan tree and a mule. Then read the six signs of life: it uses energy, it grows, it responds to the world, its kind makes copies of itself, it changes over many generations, and it is made of cells.
flow.say: Here are eight things. Some are alive and some are not, and for some it is hard to say. Here are six signs of life. First guess, without the signs, which are alive.
flow.kid: Write 8 things on cards. Guess which are alive. Then read the 6 signs of life.

ask.q: Which of the eight things is the hardest to decide, and why?
good: Viruses, because they cannot live on their own.
A dry seed, because the seed does nothing.
The candle flame, because it grows and eats.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Mules are alive but cannot have babies. A virus has a code and changes over generations, but needs a host cell. A dry seed is alive and waiting.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Alive or Not activity. You write the cards and guess.

flow.do: Draw the table. For each thing, tick the signs it shows. Then decide: alive, not alive, or hard to say. Talk about the ones that disagree with your first guess.
flow.say: For each card, tick the signs it shows. A flame uses energy and grows. But does it make copies of itself, or carry a code? Count the ticks. Then decide.
flow.kid: Tick the signs each thing shows. Then decide: alive, not alive, or hard to say.

check.q: A fire uses fuel, grows and responds to the wind. Why do most scientists not call it alive?
options: It is not made of cells and does not pass on a code that can change
It is too hot
It is too small
check.why: A fire shows some signs of life, such as using energy and growing. But it has no cells, and no code that it passes on and that can change over generations. Picking 'too hot' misses that some living things live in boiling water.

flow.context: In this step, you tick the signs of life for each thing and decide.

flow.do: Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw in the table, and why scientists find it hard to agree. Ask why this matters for finding life on other worlds.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see in your table? Why do you think scientists find it hard to agree? And why does this matter when we look for life on another planet?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why. Why does this matter in space?
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: it is hard to say exactly what life is. What I saw: some things showed a few signs but not all, like fire and viruses. Why: our list was made from life on Earth, so life elsewhere might not fit it. Scientists use a working idea: a self-sustaining chemical system that can evolve.
flow.think: If you found something on Mars that showed only some of the signs, what would you do next?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the table showed and why it matters for finding life elsewhere.

projects.title: Claim Check: is the news about life in space true?
projects.context: This is a three-day project about checking a news story. You pick a story about life in space, find where it came from, and sort each statement into things seen, things worked out and things guessed. Then you write a fair headline.

materials.item: a news story about life in space, printed or on a screen, chosen with a grown-up
a second source, such as a page from NASA, ISRO or a university
three coloured pencils, one for seen, one for worked out and one for guessed
paper and a pencil

projects.safety: Use the internet only with a grown-up. If you do not have the internet, use the Mars rock and K2-18 b cards from the Biosignature Detectives game.

schedule.what: Choose a news story about life in space. Read it with a grown-up. List what it claims.
Find the original source and a second source. Mark each claim as seen, worked out or guessed.
Write a fair headline and a short summary. Give a confidence score from 1 to 5.

projects.record: A list of claims, each marked seen, worked out or guessed. A fair headline. A confidence score from 1 to 5 with a reason.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up reading a news story on a screen with the headline 'Signs of life found on a far planet'.
setup.caption: 1. Read a news story about life in space with a grown-up.

setup.art: A page with three coloured highlighter marks on a list of claims: seen in red, worked out in green, guessed in blue.
setup.caption: 2. Mark each claim: seen, worked out or guessed.

setup.art: A child writing a fair headline on a sheet of paper, with a scale from 1 to 5 beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Write a fair headline and give a confidence score.

flow.do: With a grown-up, choose a news story about life in space. Good choices are the 2023 K2-18 b story or the 2024 Mars leopard-spot rock. Read the headline and the first three paragraphs. List every claim in the story.
flow.say: Today we choose a news story about life in space. Read the headline first. Then read the first three paragraphs. What does the story say? List every claim you can find, one by one.
flow.kid: Choose a news story about life in space. List what it says.

ask.q: Does the headline say more than the story does?
good: The headline says 'life found', but the story says 'a hint'.
The headline is more exciting than the facts.
I do not know yet.

flow.parent: Without the internet, use the Mars rock and K2-18 b cards from Biosignature Detectives. Headlines often say more than the scientists did. Notice the words 'may', 'could' and 'hint'.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Claim Check project. You choose a story and list its claims.

flow.do: Find where the story came from: a NASA page, an ISRO page, a university page or a scientific paper. Find one more source. Mark each claim in your list: seen, worked out, or guessed. Note any that the two sources disagree about.
flow.say: Now find where the story came from. Is there a page from NASA or from a university? Find a second source too. For each claim, ask: did someone see this? Did someone work it out from what they saw? Or is it a guess?
flow.kid: Find where the story came from. Mark each claim: seen, worked out, or guessed.
flow.wait: Do this on the second day

check.q: A story says 'a gas that life makes was found on a far planet'. A paper says 'we saw a hint of a gas'. Which is better evidence?
options: The paper, because it says exactly what was seen and how sure the team is
The story, because it is more exciting
Both are the same
check.why: The paper is closer to the observation and says how sure the team is. Stories often leave out the 'hint' and the doubts. Picking 'more exciting' mixes up exciting with true.

flow.context: In this step, you find the original source and mark each claim as seen, worked out or guessed.

flow.do: Write a fair headline that says only what was seen and how sure the scientists are. Write a short summary of three sentences. Give the story a confidence score from 1 to 5. Write the reason for your score.
flow.say: Now write your own headline, one that says only what was really seen. Then write three sentences of summary. Last, give the story a score from one to five for how sure we can be. Why that score?
flow.kid: Write a fair headline. Write 3 sentences. Give a score from 1 to 5.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day
flow.parent: A good fair headline for K2-18 b could be: Telescope sees a hint of a gas that life makes on Earth, but other teams disagree. A good score is low, such as 2, and a good reason is that other teams do not agree.
flow.think: How would you change your score if three more teams repeated the observation and all saw the same?
flow.context: In this step, you write a fair headline and a summary, and give a confidence score.

challenges.title: Catch the Plume: design a sampler to catch drops from a jet
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about how spacecraft sample the jets of Enceladus. A spray bottle stands for the jet. Your task is to design a collector that catches as many drops as possible as it moves past, the way Cassini flew through the plumes.
challenges.problem: A spray bottle shoots a plume of coloured water. Design a collector that you carry past the plume at a steady walking speed, 30 centimetres from the nozzle. It must catch as many coloured drops as it can, in one pass.
constraints: The collector may be at most 15 centimetres across.
You must walk past at a steady pace, taking about 3 seconds, and must not stop.
A helper gives exactly 5 sprays from the bottle during one pass.
The collector must be held at 30 centimetres from the nozzle, and not touch it.
materials: a spray bottle with water and a few drops of food colour
white paper, kitchen towel, cling film, foil and card
a tray or an old sheet to catch spills
general: A flat sheet of white paper held up in front of the plume, to catch drops on its surface.
A card with a rim or lip around the edge to stop the drops running off.
A sheet of kitchen towel that soaks up drops, so they cannot bounce away.
creative: A cone or funnel that points towards the plume, to gather drops from a wide area.
Two collectors, one for large drops and one for tiny mist, joined together.
A collector with a soft surface that stops drops from bouncing, such as folded cloth.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it. Walk past the plume once and count the coloured drops. Change one thing and test again. Which design caught the most? Why do you think it did?

setup.art: A spray bottle on a table, with a plume of coloured water in the air and a child holding a white card.
setup.caption: 1. A spray bottle makes the plume. A child walks past with a collector.

setup.art: Three drawn collector designs on paper: a flat card with a lip, a cone and a towel strip.
setup.caption: 2. Sketch three designs before building.

setup.art: A white sheet with a scatter of coloured dots, and a grid drawn over it for counting.
setup.caption: 3. Count the coloured dots in a 5 centimetre square.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Explain that Cassini flew through the plumes of Enceladus at very high speed and caught tiny grains. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs.
flow.say: The spacecraft Cassini flew through the jets of Enceladus and caught tiny pieces of ice. Our spray bottle is the jet. How would you catch as many drops as possible? Sketch two or three designs first.
flow.kid: A spray bottle is the jet. Sketch 3 ways to catch the drops.

ask.q: What would make a collector catch more drops?
good: A bigger surface.
A surface that soaks up drops.
A lip, so drops do not run off.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Catch the Plume challenge. You sketch your designs.

flow.do: Build your first design. A helper holds the spray bottle and gives 5 sprays while you walk past at a steady pace. Count the coloured drops on your collector in a 5 centimetre square. Write the number.

flow.kid: Build a collector. Walk past the plume. Count the coloured drops.
flow.parent: Do this on a tray or outside, and use only water with food colour. The helper keeps the nozzle pointing away from faces. This first number is the one to beat.

flow.do: Change one thing about your collector, such as adding a lip, or a different surface. Test it again in the same way. Write the number.

check.q: Why change only one thing at a time between tests?
options: So you know which change made the difference
So the test takes longer
So every collector looks the same
check.why: If you changed two things, you would not know which one caught more drops. One change at a time shows what each change does.

flow.context: In this step, you improve your collector and test it again.

flow.do: Compare your tests. Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it worked. Ask why a real spacecraft's collector has to work so quickly.
flow.say: Which design caught the most? What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it worked? A real spacecraft flies through the plume in seconds. Why does it have to catch everything in one pass?
flow.kid: Which design caught the most? Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: a collector that soaks up drops and has a lip catches the most. What I saw: the towel caught more than the flat card, and the card with a lip caught more than the plain card. Why: drops bounce and run off a smooth flat surface. A real spacecraft flies through a plume in a few seconds and has no second chance, so its instruments must work in one pass.
flow.think: What would you want to find out from the drops if they really came from an ocean on another world?
flow.context: In this step, you compare your tests and say what worked and why.

challenges.problem: You are in charge of a space agency. You have 10 coins to spend. Choose one or two missions that fit your budget, from five worlds. Explain your choice using what you know about water, energy and how easy it is to test.
constraints: You have 10 coins. You may spend them on one or two missions.
You must give at least three reasons for your choice: one about liquid water, one about energy and one about how easy it would be to test for life.
You must say what would change your mind.
You must say what the mission will bring back or measure.

Choose Mars, where rovers are already working and rock samples are already waiting.

Choose a mission to Titan, to test whether life could use something other than water.
Spend nothing on a new mission, and use the money to study the samples already collected.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Which World Gets the Mission challenge. You set out the five worlds and their costs.

check.q: A plan says: choose Enceladus, because its plumes carry ocean water to a spacecraft. Which of the three required reasons is that?
options: How easy it is to test
Energy
Liquid water
check.why: The plume means a spacecraft can sample the ocean without landing or drilling, which makes testing easy. The ocean itself would be the reason about liquid water, and hot rock or hydrogen in the plume the reason about energy.

flow.context: In this step, you choose your mission and write your reasons.

flow.do: Read your plan to a grown-up or a friend. Ask them to choose a different mission and give their reasons. Compare the reasons. Say whose reasons were stronger, and why.

quiz.p: Which three things does a world need before life as we know it can live there?
opts: Liquid water, a supply of energy and the right chemicals
A thick atmosphere, sunlight and a moon
Gold, iron and oxygen
quiz.why: All the life found so far needs liquid water, energy and the chemicals its body is built from. The energy can come from sunlight or from chemicals. Picking 'sunlight' alone misses the life at deep-sea vents, which lives in the dark.

quiz.p: Mercury is closer to the Sun than Venus, but Venus is hotter. Why is Venus so hot?
opts: Its thick carbon dioxide air holds heat in
Venus is bigger than Mercury
Venus has more water than Mercury
quiz.why: A world's temperature depends on its air as well as its distance. Venus's thick carbon dioxide traps heat. Picking 'more water' misses that Venus is dry and very hot.

quiz.p: A planet could go round a bright star or a dim star, at the same distance. Which statement is correct?
opts: It is warmer around the bright star, because the bright star gives out more light
It is warmer around the dim star
It is the same around both
quiz.why: A planet gets more light from a bright star at the same distance, so it is warmer. That is why the habitable zone of a dim star is closer in.

quiz.p: Bacteria at a deep-sea vent make food from hydrogen sulfide. What does this show?
opts: Life can get energy from chemicals, without sunlight
Bacteria cannot live without light
Hydrogen sulfide is food for plants
quiz.why: Chemosynthesis shows that life can live in the dark if there is a chemical source of energy. This is why scientists consider the oceans of icy moons.

quiz.p: Europa is far outside the Sun's habitable zone, but may have a liquid ocean under its ice. Why?
opts: Jupiter's pull warms the moon from inside
The Sun warms its ocean through the ice
Europa has a thick atmosphere
quiz.why: Jupiter's pull squeezes Europa a little more and a little less as it goes round, which heats it inside. The habitable zone is not the only place where liquid water can be.

quiz.p: A sealed bottle of sugar water and living yeast has a balloon that swells. What is the balloon a sign of?
opts: A gas made by the yeast
Heat in the bottle
Air that was already inside
quiz.why: Yeast eat sugar and give out carbon dioxide gas. The bottle without yeast stayed flat, which shows the gas comes from the yeast. Picking 'air that was already inside' misses that the balloon on the bottle without yeast did not swell.

quiz.p: Oxygen and methane react and would disappear from a planet's air. If both stay there, what does this suggest?
opts: Something keeps making them, perhaps life
The planet has no air
The gases cannot react
quiz.why: A mix that should fade, yet stays, is being refilled. On Earth the refilling is done by plants, algae and microbes. Scientists check that non-living chemistry cannot do the same.

quiz.p: A star dims by a tiny amount every 6 days. What is the best explanation?
opts: A planet crosses in front of the star once every 6 days
The star turns off every 6 days
The star moves away and back
quiz.why: A planet in front of its star blocks a little light. If this repeats every 6 days, the planet's year is 6 days. Picking 'turns off' misses that the dip is tiny and exactly repeating.

quiz.p: Starlight that has passed through a planet's air is missing certain colours. What can scientists work out from this?
opts: Which gases are in the air
How big the planet is
How many moons it has
quiz.why: Each gas takes away its own set of colours. So the missing colours show which gases the light passed through.

quiz.p: A planet's air has lots of oxygen. Why is that not proof of life?
opts: Strong starlight can split water and make oxygen with no life
Oxygen is not a gas
Only methane can be made by life
quiz.why: Oxygen can be made in non-living ways on some planets. Scientists look for several signs that fit together, not just one gas.

quiz.p: In a Drake chain, one set of guesses gave 100 million civilisations and another gave less than one. What does that tell us?
opts: The answer depends mostly on the guesses we know least about
The chain gives the exact answer
There are exactly 100 million civilisations
quiz.why: The steps about how often life starts and becomes intelligent are unknown, so different guesses give very different answers. The chain shows what we most need to find out.

quiz.p: A fire grows and uses fuel, but most scientists do not call it alive. Why?
opts: It has no cells and no code that it passes on and that can change over generations
Fires are too hot
Fires are too short-lived
quiz.why: A fire shows some signs of life, but it does not carry and pass on a code that changes over many generations. Picking 'too hot' misses that some living things live in boiling water.

quiz.p: A headline says 'Life found on Mars'. The scientists say, 'We found a rock with unusual spots.' Which is the better guide to what was actually seen?
opts: The scientists' own report of what was seen
The headline, because it is exciting
Neither, because both are the same
quiz.why: The scientists' report is closer to the observation and usually says how sure they are. Headlines often say more than the evidence does.

quiz.p: Why do scientists ask other teams to repeat a claim of life?
opts: To check that the sign is real and not an error
To make the claim sound more exciting
To save money
quiz.why: A result seen by only one team may be a mistake. If different teams, with different instruments, see the same thing, it is much more believable.

applications: Bread, idli, dosa and curd all depend on tiny living things that change the food and give out gas, which is the same sign scientists look for on other worlds.
The transit method that finds planets also lets astronomers study stars that pulse or have spots.
Spectra, the colours missing from light, are used to test the purity of water, the content of foods and the gases in smoke.
Telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope read the air of faraway planets from the colours missing in starlight.
Gas sensors for carbon dioxide and methane are used on farms, in landfills and in food packaging to detect living microbes.
Enzymes from microbes that live in hot springs and cold seas are used in laboratories, in detergents and in medicine.
Clean rooms for space probes use the same methods as hospitals, so that Earth germs are not carried to other worlds.
Satellite pictures of Earth show forests turning green in the monsoon, which is how living things can be seen from space.
Fermi estimates, chains of rough guesses like the Drake chain, are used to count tigers, to plan hospitals and to guess the size of a crowd.
ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission, which reached Mars in 2014, carried a sensor to look for methane in the Martian air.
Planetary protection rules for spacecraft are shared between space agencies of many countries.
Radio telescopes in India, such as the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune, listen to the sky for faint natural signals.

open_questions.q: Is there life anywhere beyond Earth, even a microbe?
open_questions.why_open: No life has been found yet. Scientists have only looked at a few places, and the best places, like the oceans under the ice of Europa and Enceladus, have not been sampled.

open_questions.q: Did life begin more than once, or only once on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: All life on Earth shares one family tree. We cannot tell if life began many times and only one family survived, because we have only one example.

open_questions.q: What made the leopard-spot rock on Mars?
open_questions.why_open: The spots may have formed with the help of microbes or by chemistry alone. The sample is still on Mars, and laboratories on Earth have not studied it.

open_questions.q: Where does the methane on Mars come from?
open_questions.why_open: Spacecraft have measured different amounts at different times. Nobody knows if it comes from rocks, from old ice, or from life.

open_questions.q: Could life use a liquid other than water, such as the methane of Titan?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found such life, and nobody has shown it is impossible. We know only one kind of life.

open_questions.q: Why have we not heard from anyone, if the galaxy has so many stars?
open_questions.why_open: We have listened to a small part of the sky for a short time. There are many possible answers, including that life is rare, and none has been tested.

maths.problem: In a made-up yeast test, the string round balloon A measured 4 centimetres at 10 minutes, 10 at 20 minutes, 16 at 30 minutes and 22 at 40 minutes. How much did it grow from 10 minutes to 40 minutes? How much did it grow on average in each 10 minutes?
maths.answer: 18 centimetres in all, and 6 centimetres in each 10 minutes.
maths.explain: 22 take away 4 is 18. From 10 minutes to 40 minutes there are 3 gaps of 10 minutes. 18 divided by 3 is 6. You can check it: 4, 10, 16, 22 go up by 6 each time.
maths.context: In the Bottle Biosignature test, you wrap a string round each balloon every 10 minutes to see how fast the gas builds up.

chart.title: Made-up example: size round balloon A

maths.why_maths: Finding the growth in each step shows how fast the yeast make gas. A steady rate is a clue that something is steadily making it.

maths.problem: A planet's year is 4 days long. A star is watched for 60 days. How many times does the planet cross in front of the star?
maths.explain: Each crossing comes once every 4 days. 60 divided by 4 is 15. You can check it by counting in fours: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60. That is 15 fours.
maths.context: In the Planet Hunter's Graph, you find a planet by the dips in a star's light. The dips repeat once in each of the planet's years.
maths.why_maths: Counting how often the dips repeat tells astronomers how sure they can be that the dips come from a planet and not from chance.

maths.problem: A message sent to a star 40 light-years away travels at the speed of light. If someone there replied at once, how many years would pass before you got the answer?
maths.explain: The message takes 40 years to get there. The reply takes 40 years to come back. 40 plus 40 is 80 years. You would need to wait a lifetime for the answer.
maths.context: This is about listening for signals from other stars. Light and radio waves take years to cross the huge distances between stars.
maths.why_maths: Adding the two journeys shows why a conversation with another star would be very slow.

maths.problem: A Drake chain starts with 100,000,000,000 stars. It divides by 5, then by 10, then by 100. How many are left?
maths.explain: 100,000,000,000 divided by 5 is 20,000,000,000. Divided by 10 is 2,000,000,000. Divided by 100 is 20,000,000. That is 20 million. You can check by multiplying back: 20,000,000 times 100 times 10 times 5 is 100,000,000,000.
maths.context: In the Drake Chain activity, you follow a chain of guesses from the number of stars to the number of civilisations.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by 10 and 100 moves the digits, and shows how quickly a number shrinks along the chain.

maths.problem: Light travels about 9.5 trillion kilometres in a year. Round that to 10 trillion. About how far is a star 40 light-years away?
maths.explain: 40 times 10 trillion is 400 trillion. You can think of it as 4 times 10, which is 40, and then multiply by 10 again to get 400. The exact answer is a little smaller, about 380 trillion, because 9.5 is a little less than 10.
maths.context: This is about how far away other stars are. Astronomers measure the distances to stars in light-years.
maths.why_maths: Rounding to 10 trillion makes the sum easy, and it is good enough to show how huge the distance is.

maths.problem: In a made-up curd test, cup C in the warm box set after 5 hours, and cup B on the counter set after 11 hours. How many hours longer did cup B take? Did cup C take more or less than half of cup B's time?
maths.answer: 6 hours longer. Cup C took a little less than half.
maths.explain: 11 take away 5 is 6 hours. Half of 11 hours is 5 and a half hours. Cup C took 5 hours, which is a little less than 5 and a half. So warmth made the curd set in about half the time.
maths.context: In the Curd Zones test, you put the same milk and curd in different places and see how long each takes to set.
maths.why_maths: Comparing times shows how much warmth speeds up tiny living things, which helps us guess where life could grow quickly.

maths.problem: Venus is about 460 degrees on the surface. Mars is about minus 60 degrees. How many degrees hotter is Venus than Mars?
maths.explain: From minus 60 up to 0 is 60 degrees. From 0 up to 460 is another 460 degrees. 60 plus 460 is 520 degrees. So Venus is 520 degrees hotter than Mars.
maths.context: This is about Venus and Mars, two planets next to Earth. One is far too hot and the other is far too cold.
maths.why_maths: Counting up through zero is how you find the gap between a hot world and a cold one. Venus and Mars are far apart in temperature, and the air of each planet is one of the reasons.

maths.problem: A spacecraft crosses a plume at about 8 kilometres every second. A made-up plume is 40 kilometres wide. How many seconds does the crossing take?
maths.explain: The spacecraft goes 8 kilometres each second. 40 divided by 8 is 5. You can check it: 8 times 5 is 40. So the instruments have only about 5 seconds to collect grains.
maths.context: In the Catch the Plume challenge, you collect drops from a jet as you walk past. A real spacecraft does the same, much faster.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the width by the speed shows how little time the instruments have, which is why a collector must work in one pass.

roots.context: In this unit you tested bottles of yeast and cups of curd, and learned how scientists read the air of other worlds. This part asks two things: why living things can be found by the changes they make, and how sure anyone can be about something they cannot see.

deep_truth.truth: In the Bottle Biosignature test, only the bottle with living yeast and sugar made gas and blew up its balloon. From outside, you could not see the yeast, only the gas they kept making. On a far planet, life might show up in the same way, as gases that would fade away unless living things kept making them. So we may find life by what it keeps changing, long before we see a creature.
deep_truth.habit: We expect to find life by seeing a creature. But from far away, the first sign would be a change in the air.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Bottle Biosignature test, the yeast and sugar bottle swelled the balloon on top, and the bottles with no yeast, no sugar or dead yeast stayed flat. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Each breath you breathe out holds about a hundred times more carbon dioxide than the air you breathed in. Your body changes the air around you all the time.
three.what_is_life: We cannot see yeast or curd bacteria. We know they are alive from what they do: bubbles in the batter, a lid lifted by gas, milk that sets into curd.
three.what_is_this_world: Earth's air is full of oxygen only because plants and microbes keep making it. Without them, it would fade away.

roots.thread: Living things change the world around them. Yeast change the air in a bottle. Plants and microbes keep Earth's air full of oxygen. Bacteria around a hot vent turn chemicals from the vent into food. From a distance, only these changes can be seen. So a living thing and its surroundings cannot be cleanly separated. When scientists read the air of a distant planet, they are asking whether something there keeps changing that air. What remains is the question of how sure we can be about something we cannot see.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Svetaketu to break open a banyan fruit, and then a seed inside the fruit. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing, sir.' 'This great banyan tree grows from that fine thing you cannot see.'
teachings.link: We cannot see yeast, but a swollen balloon shows they are there. The unseen shows itself by what it does.

teachings.teaching: Do not accept something only because of report, tradition or hearsay. When you know for yourselves what is good and what is harmful, then act on it.
teachings.link: A news story that says 'signs of life found' should be checked. Scientists ask what was observed and what was only guessed.

teachings.teaching: Whatever the matter, and whoever says it, wisdom is to find the true meaning in it.
teachings.link: A claim about life in space might come from a famous person or from a child. The test is the evidence, not the speaker.

science.text: Living things change the gases around them, and these changes can be measured. On Earth, plants and microbes keep both oxygen and methane in the air, though these two gases react with each other and would otherwise disappear.
A mix of gases that would not last together may be a sign of life on a far planet. Scientists are testing how often non-living chemistry can fake it.
Whether life exists on any world beyond Earth is not known.

other_view.who: Scientists who are careful about claims of life
other_view.view: Gases alone can never prove that something is alive, because non-living chemistry can make nearly every gas that life makes. Only a living sample, seen to grow and copy itself in a laboratory, would settle it. Until then, every claim should be treated as a question. That is an honest and careful view.

practice.title: Listen for what you cannot see
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Put one hand on your chest and feel your heart. Put the other hand in front of your nose and feel your breath. You cannot see your heart or your breath. How do you know they are there? Breathe slowly three times, and notice what your body is doing to the air.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Put one hand on your chest and feel your heart. Feel your breath on your other hand. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: How would you know that something is alive if you could never see it?

how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1960s, NASA planned to land spacecraft on Mars to look for life. Most scientists thought the only way was to scoop up soil and test it for living things. James Lovelock, a British scientist asked to help, thought of another way. He asked what an observer far away would learn by studying Earth's air. Earth's air holds oxygen and methane together, even though they react and should disappear. They stay because living things keep making them. Mars's air looked like a settled mix, with nothing refilling it. In 1965 Lovelock wrote that Mars was probably lifeless and that a planet's air could show life from far away. In 1967, with Dian Hitchcock, an American scientist who worked at NASA, he published a longer paper on the idea. Today, telescopes read the air of faraway planets in just this way.
how_we_found_out.who: James Lovelock, a British scientist, and Dian Hitchcock, an American scientist working with NASA
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought the only way to find out if a planet has life was to land and test its soil. Lovelock and Hitchcock showed that a planet's air, studied from far away, can reveal whether something is keeping it out of balance.
